3. Record of the children of the Gattorno spouses. — EMMANUELE, born on 21 January 1828, baptized the same day: Register of the Parish of S. Donato, year 1828, p. 61. Died at Genoa on 9 February 1873.

— The Servant of God Rosa Gattorno

— GIUSTINA, born on 6 December 1833, baptized the same day

with the names Maria Giustina Benedetta: Register of the Parish

of S. Maria delle Vigne, year 1833 p. 205.

She married Giovanni Argenti and had three children. She died at Pegli

(Genoa) on 20 November 1917.

— FEDERICO Giuseppe Agostino, born on 13 January 1836 and bap-

tized the following day: Register of the Parish of S. Maria delle

Vigne, year 1836, p. 59.

A Mazzinian and later a follower of Garibaldi, in whose army he rose

to the rank of colonel, he took part in the expedition of the Thousand and

in other famous battles; he was enrolled in Freemasonry. He was a per-

son of great honesty and generosity. He was of great help to his sis-

ter Rosa in many affairs of the Institute. Through the influence of the

Servant of God he secretly contracted a religious marriage with his

companion Amelia Aloi on 21 November 1885 in Rome, in the cha-

pel of the Daughters of St. Anne in Vicolo del Piombo. The marriage

is narrated by an eyewitness (cf. Memoirs of Sr. A. Celsa

Speranza 3.2, B. 3.78), but it is not found registered in the Ro-

man parishes concerned (S. Martino ai Monti; Santi XII Apostoli)

nor in the Vicariate, not even among the secret marriages.

He had no children. He died in Rome on 17 June 1913.

— ELISA, born at Genoa on 25 June 1838, baptized the following day with the names Caterina Luigia Adelaide: Register of the Parish of S. Maria delle Vigne, year 1838, no. 105.

She married Angelo Savignone and had seven children. The eldest, Adele, entered the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne taking the name Sr. A. Francesca and died in the odor of sanctity on 24 June 1884 at Piacenza.

— Francesco Giustino, born at Genoa on 15 May 1843 and baptized the following day: Register of the Parish of S. Maria delle Vigne, year 1843 no. 89.

He married Clotilde Marchesi and had two children. He assiduously helped the Servant of God in the affairs of the Institute, giving proof of great honesty. He died at Genoa on 30 July 1922.

10. Attestation of good conduct during the period of widowhood; AFSA: A.1.4.

A significant document because it summarizes the many works of zeal of the Servant of God in this period.

Attestation of Morality

I, the undersigned, attest that Mrs. Rosa Gattorno, widow Custo, for about 12 years, that is, from the time she became a widow, came to live in this Parish, where she dwelt for eight successive years in her parents' house, during which time she distinguished herself by works of piety and charity, frequenting the Sacraments, assisting the sick, instructing in Christian Doctrine the ignorant girls in the public oratories, striving to obtain alms for them from wealthy persons, taking into safe places girls in danger or already fallen, working and engaging other pious Ladies to work in order to provide the necessary furnishings for poor churches.

In short, the undersigned can assure that the said Lady was, in this period of time, of private and public edification.

In witness whereof, from the Metropolitan of S. Lorenzo in Genoa, 25 August 1869.

Can. STEFANO PARODI

Seen etc.

13. Letter appointing the Servant of God Vice-President of the commission for endangered girls, 7 January 1865; AFSA: A.1.4.

Genoa, 7 [January] 1865

Most esteemed Madam

On behalf of the Council of the pious Association of Ladies for the growth of the Catholic Faith, I am writing to inform you that it has formed a Commission for girls endangered in their morals, of which Your Most Esteemed Ladyship is a member.

14. Holograph will of the Servant of God, 20 November 1899; AFSA: A.1.4.

In the Name of the Most Holy Trinity, Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

To avoid any misunderstanding arising after my death, I have decided to make my Holograph Will and therefore I dispose as follows.

At the feet of my dear Crucifix I beg my dear daughters of St. Anne not to trouble themselves over my funeral and transfer, but only to carry out what our Constitutions prescribe.

I must further declare that everything that came both from my Paternal Patrimony and from my family's, I have already handed over entirely, both to my late Son when he was alive, and to my Daughter married to Mr. Gaspare, Count Barbiellini Amidei, and what I have declared appears from Public Acts legally drawn up. I have reserved nothing for myself, whether of what came from my Gattorno Family or of what came from the family of my Consort, Custo.

Of the very little that belongs to me, consisting almost exclusively of worn clothing, rights, shares and claims, I name and wish to be my universal heirs my Friends and fellow sisters Mrs. Maria Anna Carrega, daughter of the late Antonio, a native of Genoa, and Mrs. Carolina Speranza, daughter of the late Costanzo, a native of Sassuolo Modenese, to whom, with the noble title of Institution, I leave my most meager inheritance. I intend to forgive whoever may in any way have offended me and done me harm, even involuntarily, just as I likewise ask pardon of all.

I bless my daughter, my Son-in-law and their children, my grandchildren, imploring from God every good. So too I wish my brothers Federico and Francesco and my Sisters Giusta and Elisa every good, both in this and in Eternal Life.

This is my Holograph Will, written, dated and signed by me.

Made in Rome this twentieth day of November one thousand eight hundred and ninety-nine - Ninety-nine, Sr. Anna Rosa Gattorno, daughter of the late Francesco, a native of Genoa.

16. Declaration of the attending physician, 8 May 1900; AFSA: A.1.4.

The undersigned declares that Mrs. A. Rosa Gattorno for about 12 years had been affected by interstitial nephritis and that for about a year she had been subject to attacks of cardiac arrhythmia due to arteriosclerosis. About three months earlier she was struck by a severe influenza and, although the renal phenomena remained in normal condition, the condition of the heart worsened so as to let the catastrophe be foreseen. Three days before death the said conditions were aggravated by a violent entero-peritonitis due in large part to the ingestion of substances hard to digest. He therefore declares that death is due exclusively to the cause of the old and recent lesions.

Rome, 8 May 1900.

Dr. MONTECHIARI

18. Declaration of Fr. Vincenzo da Alatri OFM Capp., confessor of the Servant of God, 28 May 1900; AFSA: A.1.4.

In the Name of God - Amen

I, the undersigned, Ordinary Confessor of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, located at Via Merulana no. 177, certify that the Very Reverend Mother Anna Rosa Gattorno, Foundress and first General of the aforesaid Institute, during a three-year period in which I had the honor and good fortune to approach her, always gave me proofs of an uncommon rectitude, honesty and perfection.

Endowed by God with the holiest and noblest charisms, she spent her days doing good to all and relieving from so many miseries poor languishing humanity. God, however, willed to hasten for Mother Gattorno the reward of her good deeds.

p. 706

In fact, for some years now, tormented more than usual by her continual and bitter ailments, from that time she had been giving warning that she would not last so long on this earth.

The sad foreboding, alas, came true.

The illness, which made its most rapid progress each day, was at the same time transformed in various and more painful ways; so much so that, feeling the last days of her mortal course drawing near, She who had never in life failed to confess often and to refresh herself every morning with the Bread of Angels, redoubled her fervor as death approached. She was reconciled by me several times; I made her gain the Indulgences of the Holy Jubilee, which she desired to gain again by visiting the Basilicas, should she recover her health. Moreover, by the Very Rev. Fr. Agostino Donadio of the Minims, after confession, she was devoutly given Communion.

The hour of Agony was advancing with great strides. And noticing that not much time remained before her happy passage to eternity, she was never again abandoned by me. So that for two days I remained in the House of the Institute, being replaced in the noble charity by the aforementioned Fr. Agostino during some absence of mine on account of duty.

I myself, by Apostolic authority, imparted to her the papal blessing. And, with all her companions and spiritual Daughters present, as well as the blood relatives of the Very Reverend Mother, I administered to her the Last Anointing, with all the comforts of our Holy Religion. And these comforts I prolonged until she rendered her beautiful soul to the Creator, amid the groans and tears of all present, on Sunday 6 May 1900 at about 9 in the morning. All this for the truth and justice of my Ministry, as well as for the honor and respect due to the holy soul of the Foundress of the Daughters of St. Anne, who we now hope is already in Paradise in the bosom of God, enjoying his beatific vision.

In witness whereof etc.

Rome, in the Convent of the Immaculate Conception, this day 28 May 1900.

P. VINCENZO DA ALATRI

Capuchin

Ordinary Confessor

of the Daughters of St. Anne 19. Description of the private room of the Servant of God, 24 Ju-

ne 1901; AFSA: A.1.4.

Piacenza, 24 June 1901

On the thirtieth of May of this year, the very morning on which eleven Daughters of St. Anne were to leave for South America, entrusted to Sister Anna Pacifica Bertone, sent there to carry out the office of Provincial, at a wish expressed by her, I led her to see the room where the venerated and lamented Foundress and Mother General of this Institute, Sister Anna Rosa Gattorno, spent her nights and the few hours she allowed to rest. With the two of us there asked to come the General Assistant, Sister Anna Camilla Valentini, and the Superior of the Mother House, Sister Anna Giuseppa Troni:

During the Foundress's life no one, neither sisters nor lay persons, had ever been able to set foot in that room, whose necessary cleaning she alone did, except for a judicial visit, caused by a lawsuit that had been brought against the Rev. Mother Gattorno, of pious memory, by her daughter-in-law, Maria Tellini.

This, however, happened at a time when the Mother herself was in Rome and by breaking the locks, since the key to the door always remained with her.

What we four saw in that room took on such importance in our eyes as to put us in serious embarrassment about how to conduct ourselves in future. Hence, after mature reflection, we came to the decision to turn to the counsel of a prudent and authoritative person; and, since Providence offered him to us in His Excellency the Most Rev. Bishop Scalabrini, whose prudence and loftiness of mind are beyond dispute, I, accompanied by the aforesaid assistant, went to him to ask for the desired precious counsel.

He, kind and charitable as always, let me explain the purpose of our visit and mention our concerns. Then he advised us not to speak of the matter to a living soul; to make a detailed and conscientious report of the room and of what it contains; and afterward to lock it with a key to prevent anyone else from entering. He then added that we should hand him a copy of that report, about which also the most scrupulous silence must be kept.

p. 708

And it is to follow this counsel, as wise as any other, that on the morning of the 16th instant I, the Secretary General, Sister Anna Celsa Speranza, and the Assistant Sister Anna Camilla Valentini entered the room: we went three of us, so that nothing found there might escape our observation.

The little room is on the mezzanine and looks onto the glass-paned roof that covers the laundry.

It is reached by a steep little wooden staircase, 0.51 m wide, which also gives access to the choir loft of the Chapel by means of a few steps that branch off, at its top, on the right side.

A small door, which barely lets one person through and which closes with a single-leaf door, gives access to the little room.

With the little door open one sees first a screen about a meter and a half high, made of six frames covered with paper wallpaper and joined together with hinges. This screen divides the rectangular little room almost across its whole width into two parts, thus forming with it and with the wall in which the small entrance door is set a sort of little corridor; so that whoever enters this first part of the room cannot see what is in the other. When the screen is folded, a spectacle presents itself to the eye of the visitor so moving in its immense grandeur that it cannot fail to inspire in his soul such a feeling of admiration and deep piety as to oblige him to prostrate himself on the ground and burst into sobs.

The small room measures 6.07 m in length, 3.04 m in width and 2.87 m in height. Its walls are unplastered and crumbling from damp. Two narrow, low windows with several broken panes light it. The ceiling, which is vaulted, is cracked in various places and from it hangs, like a canopy, a quantity of very dense cobwebs. The floor is of bricks.

So much for the space of the room, from which breathes an air of poverty, humility and penitence so great that it edifies.

For all furniture there is an iron bedstead, of the most primitive and simple kind, painted green; it holds a straw mattress of very coarse, raw cloth, filled with corn husks.

This was the bed! On the headboard, on the right side, is a coconut rosary of seven decades, from which hangs a medal bearing on one side the image of St. Michael, on the other that of the Virgo Potens.

In front of the second window — taking the entrance door as the starting point — there is a rough little rectangular table, on whose top are: an ebony case lined with red plush, inside which a Crucifix is kept (Regarding this Crucifix, please read the declaration attached to this one); a very modest glass inkwell, empty; a pen-holder and a pencil; and in a corner on the right side a piece of soap.

In the drawer of the little table, as wide and long as the table itself, are found:

A gimlet, a file, pincers and wire;

Two wide and tall bracelets, two medium and two small ones of braided iron wire with markedly rough protrusions;

Various pieces of a small brass chain;

A broken mother-of-pearl medallion, representing the baptism of Jesus;

A small relic, wrapped in a little piece of paper;

Two medals, one bearing the image of Pius IX, the other that of Our Lady of the Stars;

A silver medal, wrapped in a paper on which are written these precise words in the hand of the lamented Foundress: Medal received from Pius IX who kept it in his pocket for 10 years. The medal bears on one side the image of Our Lady of Good Counsel; on the other that of the Most Holy Crucifix venerated at Genazzano;

Another small metal Crucifix, which still bears the marks of dried blood and flesh: it is wrapped in a paper on whose inner side are the following words, written by Mother Rosa Gattorno: «Dear Crucifix It stayed five years and more inside my flesh on the side of the Heart so that it could no longer be seen the spasms were terrible and spasmodic was the pain Jesus wanted me to take it out which I suffered I fainted once I had taken it out it seemed to me I was deprived of everything But so wished my beloved and I obeyed. The wound never healed it was so deep and a heap of grown flesh was around it My God what to do? It gave me a great deal of blood I went saying between me and myself so will it go gangrenous? What must I do? I would sooner die than say it because I would never allow any doctor to look at me I put cold plasters on it and at the end of a year it began to heal and no longer gave blood and the grown flesh came off by itself. My beloved I always said to him you have done me so much harm heal me so that no one can notice it. I took it off in 1864».

Another little piece of paper, also found in the drawer, contains a Blessing of St. Francis with two little pieces of cloth for use as relics.

On the window sill, between the wall and the shutter of the window itself, is a glass tumbler of the most ordinary kind.

In the corner of the room, which is a short distance from the little table, there is a washstand of raw wood with a basin of baked clay painted green; and at the foot of the washstand, set on the floor, is a very ordinary clay pitcher.

In the corner opposite this one is an old broom.

Leaning against the facing wall on entering are two chairs: one with a seat of fine rush, of the kind bought from furniture dealers; the other of soft raw wood, seated with common rush, just such as the peasants make in the idle days of winter.

On the left side of the bed is a rough wooden prie-dieu, which has two drawers: one in the upper part, where the arms rest; the other in the lower, on which one kneels.

On the upper surface of the prie-dieu are: A natural death's head; a small glass tumbler for use as a night lamp; and a little box of night-lights.

Inside the drawer in the lower part is a chamber pot of ordinary baked clay.

Not far from the prie-dieu, going toward the wall where the entrance door is, a niche has been made in the wall. This has at the bottom a brick step serving as a kneeler, and, at the height of a little over a meter, a shelf also made of bricks. Right in the middle of the niche a little window has been made, now stopped up with the 2nd volume of the Complete Works of St. John of the Cross. We, the undersigned, declare for the plain truth, ready also to take an oath on it, that we have heard several times, told in confidence by the late Rev. our Mother Foundress, Sister Anna Rosa Gattorno, the following, regarding the Crucifix listed among the objects on the table top in her private little room.

From her youth Rosa Gattorno had a special veneration for this Crucifix, which, hung on the cross fixed in the pedestal now found in the niche of the aforesaid little room, she always kept in her room.

She was still in the world when one evening, while she was praying fervently, kneeling with her head bowed between her hands before the Crucifix, it detached itself from the wood; and, passing over her head, fell onto her shoulders. She picked it up and put it back in place, nailing it again. The event was repeated the following evening; and she nailed it again, and this time as firmly as she could. The third evening the Crucifix detached itself again; and Gattorno, thinking then that those nails no longer held, called her maid and entrusted her with the task of nailing the Crucifix to the wood using rather long and sturdy nails. And so it was done. But the event being repeated afterward, she, perhaps by God's inspiration, concluded that the Crucifix no longer wished to remain hanging on the cross; and so she wrapped it in a linen cloth. She kept it thus until, after several years as Foundress and Mother General of this Institute, she received as a gift from her intimate friend, the Most Illustrious Princess Emilia di Fitalia, of Palermo, to whom she had one day given her Crucifix to kiss, a most beautiful ebony case, specially made, with the request to keep it in it. The Illustrious Lady had felt such devout compassion for the Crucifix, wrapped in that humble cloth, that she did not want it to remain there any longer; and she had immediately thought of providing the case.

The wooden Cross from which the Crucifix hung is found in the Sacristy of the Mother House and presently serves in the Good Friday ceremonies.

We also attest that we have heard it told by a trustworthy person that the Crucifix in question spoke to Gattorno when she was barely seven years old.

B - DOCUMENTS RELATING TO THE RELIGIOUS VOCATION

AND FOUNDATION OF THE INSTITUTE

1. The foundation of the Institute according to the account of the Servant of God, extract from the Memoirs 2, pp. 1-60; AFSA: A.3.30.

For easier reading the document is divided into several parts; the headings belong to the editors.

Correction of Frassinetti's rule and first inspiration

In February 1864, out of obedience, I was put at the head of the Congregation of the daughters of Mary, whose Director was Frassinetti, and he had made the rules. Not knowing any more how to go forward, that priest went to my confessor to beg him to tell me to accept such an assignment. My confessor let himself be moved by Frassinetti's tears and promised him that I would accept, because he would command it of me by virtue of holy obedience. So it happened. I must say that when that priest came to me, seeing him weep I was confused and promised to put his work in order and that I would take the whole task upon myself, but first I wanted to hear the opinion of my archbishop as to how I should proceed and whether he was pleased that I should take it on. Then Frassinetti told me that the archbishop permitted such a work but did not want to approve the rules, begging me to obtain such approval. «Very well,» I answered him (a little confused), fearing that the archbishop was opposed. We agreed that I would take the rules to the archbishop and would act according to what he decided.

p. 715

The next day I went to the feet of the most excellent prelate and set before him in order and clearly what Frassinetti had told me and what my confessor had commanded me, that I had reserved to hear his counsel and that on this alone depended my accepting definitively, and I gave him the rules, and as soon as he saw them he told me that he knew them and did not want to approve them unless what he did not like was removed from them. I begged him to tell me what he wished removed. He answered me: «But will Frassinetti submit to this?» «Yes — I answered him — because if he does not, I shall not accept being what he wants.» «Very well — he answered me — one thing more I want in order to give this approval: I want you to guess what displeases me in these rules.» «My God, how shall I do it?» «Go, and you will return when you have made the notes.» He would hear no more and, confused, I went home. But! How shall I be able to guess?

Having reached my room I put these rules under the feet of my dear Crucifix: «Think about it, my Love, if I must obey, you suggest it to me» and I thought no more of it. Night came, well advanced; I took my dear Crucifix and the rules into my arms: «Tell me, my Love: where are the difficulties to be removed?» So in that position I remained in rapture and a voice told me what I must remove, the archbishop being right not to approve them with those maxims, because it was not God's will. Having recovered, I kissed and thanked my Beloved and at once went to the table, leafing through that little book, and on a sheet I wrote down everything exactly as my God had dictated to me.

When I had finished I felt so beside myself that I folded everything up and then, taking my dear Crucifix again, I thanked him. «Oh! — I pressed him to my breast — my Love!» That said, behold, I was again rapt in ecstasy and I clearly felt that He himself was dictating a rule to me. So he told me and what he dictated to me was so clear, and it seemed that this dictation had a different effect on me. «Write at once what I have told you!» These were the last words and, having recovered, I did not delay to obey. I wrote down exactly what he had dictated to me and, having put it away safely, I went back to pray, and nothing gave me concern.

The next day, without saying anything, I went to Frassinetti to find out whether he was content that the archbishop had removed what the archbishop did not like and that, if he submitted, the archbishop would approve his rules. With pleasure he answered me that he was ready to accept any amendment and that I should tell the archbishop to remove what he did not like, and that he submitted to everything. In fact, after a few days I went to the archbishop and told him what Frassinetti had told me and (without telling him anything of how it had happened) I gave him the corrections which I had above in the little book, and he, with surprise, told me that they were exactly those that he wished removed, and I copied them out, returning them to him and, his approval having been put on them, I handed them to Frassinetti, who was beside himself with joy, but no one knew anything of what had happened.

First resistance and the regulation of Canon Magnasco

Those [rules] that I had put away began to disturb me, because an inner voice always tormented me, telling me that I must have them seen, that it was His work, but I drove it away and, to put it better, I did not understand what he wanted. One evening: «What do you want, my dear Crucifix? Why must I have this writing seen? What is it to serve for?» He answered me: «For the work that I want, great it will be!»

My God! I began to think and understood nothing. Where is it to be, who is to do this work? I felt so confused that I gave up the thought and began to pray, clasped to my dear Crucifix, and a voice that was certainly His, my Beloved's, said to me: «From you I want this work. Take to the archbishop the writing you have.» Oh! how my mind was thrown into confusion! «Another work, how to undertake it? What shame to say this to the archbishop! Oh! my God, I feel that my strength does not suffice to do what you command me, I feel I am dying at the mere thought of it. And my children, my mother» and I wept. «No, my Jesus, I do not have the courage; I cannot!» and I went on weeping for several days, but never made up my mind.

At last I revealed it to the confessor under the seal of confession, but as soon as he heard this he gave me a good scolding and then commanded me to go at once to the archbishop. Weeping, I asked him to allow me to write everything to him and send him a copy of the writing. He approved what I asked and at once he too wished to read it and then, with my letter in which I told him the matter, I sent it to the archbishop. As soon as he had read it he wrote to me to come to him. I cannot describe my confusion, the pain; I trembled like a leaf, I was so agitated that on reaching his feet there was no way I could speak. He noticed my state and, knowing my temperament, limited himself to telling me to try to put into execution the Lord's orders and that the work would certainly be very beautiful, only that it was necessary to weave an internal regulation over them. I, confused, answered yes to everything, when again he called me after a few days and told me that he would send Magnasco, who at that time was Canon penitentiary, so that together with him I might make this regulation.

In fact he came and tried to put something in order, but inwardly I felt it was not what Jesus wanted, and so it happened that Magnasco took this regulation to the archbishop and he did not like it at all. He sent for me and asked me whether I liked them. I was confused, I did not want to say anything, but he ordered me to speak and to say frankly what I had had and what I found was not right. He, before I spoke, said: «I do not like them; very well, I want you to mark them with your fingernail, so that he will not notice the correction, since they are not right.» I took them up again and lightly marked with my fingernail the chapters that were all to be cancelled, and with a letter of mine I sent them back to the archbishop, who sent for me telling me that nothing would be done with that regulation, since he too saw that it did not agree with the rules received from my God.

The audience with Pius IX

I took courage and begged him that before trying to make a regulation I wanted to hear His Holiness Pope Pius IX, because I hoped that the Holy Father would take the obedience away from me and would certainly give such a charge to another, or else everything would go up in the air, nothing more would be done. I set out my doubts to him, telling him that it could be a diabolical art, since I had two children and a very old father and mother to whom I was very attached, and I could not do this, leave them, no. My children, then, the mere thought of having to leave them was torture, and I repeated to myself: «No, it will never be, no.» The good Shepherd granted me that I might go to Rome, furnishing me with letters of recommendation.

It seemed to me that I had already won the victory. «Never (I kept repeating to myself) will Pope Pius IX permit a mother to leave her children, and a mother to whom I bore an immense affection, also to the poor old father, who both loved me so much and, one may say, in the last years adored me.» «Oh! no, my Love! you will not permit it. Your Vicar will give me peace and relief in so cruel a battle. His word will be for me a balm on the wound of grief bitterly opened.»

I made this wish known to my parents, and they, poor things, agreed with pleasure, thinking to do me a kindness, and furnished me with letters of recommendation, and poor papa found a place for me and my companion on one of the best sea steamers as far as Livorno, the railway not yet existing, only from Livorno to Civitavecchia. The boys were both in boarding school.

We left on the day before the eve of the 1st of the year 1866, I mean 28 December of the year that was ending, 1865. I arrived in Rome after having suffered horribly, because on the sea steamer, when we were near 2 after midnight, a wheel broke and the engineer gave himself up for lost, a fainting fit seized me so that I understood nothing more. The poor captain, to whom I had been so strongly recommended, was distressed, my companion was desolate; I remained several hours like this; having recovered when the steamer had been repaired and was moving, I wished to take nothing to refresh myself because I wanted to go to Livorno fasting to make Holy Communion. So it happened. Arriving at exactly noon, I had myself taken at once to a church to receive my treasure. I entrusted myself to a poor woman, giving her a good alms to have a priest come to this church; I also heard Mass because it was a feast day and there was the one o'clock afternoon Mass. My friend afterward took me to a café but I could take nothing except two cold potatoes.

She wanted me to agree to go and see Livorno, but I felt so ill that I could not bear it and so we went to the station, and after a short while we left. Arriving at Civitavecchia at 5 the next morning, I went to make Holy Communion and at once by stagecoach we went on to Rome, which we reached at one o'clock on the 1st of January 1866; we had heard Mass in a village where we stopped, which I no longer remember. I do not know how to describe what I felt. I was given a little refreshment and then at once came people who had already been told of our arrival.

The audience was requested and was held on 3 January at 5 in the afternoon; it was a private audience. Oh! I shall never forget this day! My hopes vanished and a most bitter knife came to wound me deeply.

I had already had the rules given to the Supreme Pontiff, I mean those my dear Crucifix dictated to me, which according to the Holy Father's saying were like the commandments. As soon as I was at his holy feet, Pius IX blessed me and, raising me with the hand that held mine, told me he had read those rules and that they were truly beautiful and that I must not delay putting them into execution.

Oh! I threw myself on the ground and weeping said to him: «Holiness, I have two children, an old father and mother, and both my children are small!» He answered me: «It is of no use, God wills it so.» «Oh! no, Holiness, God according to the Holy Gospel will ask me to account for my children;» — and I wept bitterly — I love them too much, I cannot leave them. «Holiness, it is impossible!»

The Holy Father stops and in a severe tone says to me: «Very well: if you do not do what God wants of you, you will have remorse for the whole time of your life, your conscience will gnaw at you and you will have no more peace.» I was frightened and: «No, Holiness — I answered him — I want to do God's will.»

He went on: «Good»; in a manner as if inspired he said to me: «This Institute will spread rapidly, like the flight of the dove, to all parts of the world.

God will take care of your children: you think of God in His work.» What a prophecy!

Dear Holy Father Pius IX!

I rose and could hardly utter a word, I felt my breast breaking. He brought me to his writing desk and gave me two photographs of himself, writing a motto on each. Oh! how I felt! nothing was a comfort to me. He went on: «Papa and mama will resign themselves. You will lack nothing, everything will be given you!» I hardly understood; he added: «These I keep, surely you will have another copy and you will think of giving them the form of a regulation.»

I had put «daughters of Mary Immaculate» in the heading because I was not only very devout but a lover and wholly of Mary. He asked me whether the title too had been given me by God. I answered him no, I had received nothing: it was my wish that they be so called, being myself also a daughter of Mary. «I know,» said the Holy Father. From his words mentioned above, whether God had also given me the title, I realized that everything had been written to him. A trembling seized me, and the Pope himself, who was holding me by the hand, and my tears kept flowing, however much strength I used.

The children's suffering. Temptation to leave everything

He began to comfort me, assuring me that my children would have a particular assistance from God, as in fact happened, for in both the hand of God was visibly seen, which governed them and with special graces kept them under his mantle. Oh! how I saw materially his protection in everything, so much so that I did not worry at all, thinking that God was taking care of their education and their placement, as happened with the daughter, and the son he always brought back when he ran away, but never allowed him to be in bad company. What he did was out of too good a heart, but he came back and made his holy Exercises with the friars, who gave me great praise of him and he knew how to make himself much loved; I cannot express the love and respect he bore me: it was something extraordinary; he always had «Mamà» on his lips: for him I was everything. I would have too much to say.

It is certain that when they imprudently told him at school that I was a nun, he went mad, the blood rushed to his head and he no longer reasoned, but I immediately had him brought to me, while I was still dressed as a lay woman. As soon as he saw me he wept, and then fixed his eyes on mine and said strongly: «Mamà! Mamà!» How to describe this event! My soul was breaking, but I did myself such violence that he noticed nothing of my distress and, shaking him, I made him observe that I was not a nun but dressed as a lay woman, and then he looked at those who were already dressed and wept. All at once he flew into a fury and wanted to strike us, not knowing what he was doing. Then I thought of having him left with me (he was not yet 11) and I took him so gently that he made a little retreat together with me and then Holy Communion so well that it was a consolation, and then he went back to school and gave such beautiful signs of wanting to become a priest and made his communion almost every day, and his confessor told me that I must watch over him because he tended to penances, fearing for his health.

At that time I too took the veil and he wept much when he saw me, but made no more uproar. I notice that I am off the subject and lost, and perhaps I should not narrate certain particulars which only my God knew what they cost me and how much I suffered. How many times the temptation came to me to abandon everything and go back to them! but I always repeated to myself the words that the Holy Father Pius IX said to me and, when I went to them, how I let them feel that that temptation was terrible for me; but the thought of acting against God's will made me resist any martyrdom, and I repeated to myself: «I shall have no more peace; all the time of my life my conscience will gnaw at me forever.» What words, and spoken by the Holy Father with such seriousness!

The offering before the image of Our Lady of Sorrows

I return to the Holy Father's words when he was asking me about the title. Hearing that it was my own doing he said to me: «Good, for now let it be so; but when you have the true title, if God wishes it to be another, you will obey and at once the one the Lord assigns will be put.» I was silent, not knowing what to answer, only: «Yes, Holiness, I shall do your obedience.» With other words of encouragement he blessed me and I went home, where, shutting myself in as soon as I could finish and take leave of certain persons who were waiting for us, I began to weep and kept it up until the next day, so that I had even lost the sense of touch, my hands were numb, so the body, the head. I always repeated to myself: «My children, my Jesus! my mother and father! I do not have the courage!» — then I wept bitterly, but it was not so much the father and mother that caused me and brought me grief, no, to these it was easy to resign myself, but the children!

I went to the feet of the Virgin of Sorrows in the church of the Servites — where after their father's death I had taken them to that Most Holy Virgin and consigned them to her so resolutely that it seemed to me that She would take all the care of them, and with an inner voice assured me of it. Prostrate at the feet of this Sovereign and queen of sorrows, in copious weeping I said to her: «I must abandon my children! Your Son by means of his Vicar commands it of me. I feel torn apart by grief. I have great affection for them! You, my mother, experienced the abandonment of Jesus: the mere fact of having lost him for three days, what it cost You! Oh! my children! I do not know how to find peace. Leave them? and where, and with whom? Alas! it is too strong! How unhappy I am! I am a mother, and I bear them so much affection. Mary, Mary, my Mother! what a knife this is! it pierces me to the marrow of my bones!»

I remained absorbed; my tears dried and in the Most Holy Virgin I acquired peace, strength. Having recovered, I found myself transformed: a giant.

With generosity I made the offering to God and repeated to him the words of Abraham: «Here I am to fulfill your divine Will, and I shall never again return to complaints and almost insistence to draw back, nor to a thousand protests.» And offering myself as victim for His work, I had very great consolations and the Most Holy Virgin assured me that she will always be with me and my children will be Hers. Oh! Sweet word! (so it was).

The decision to begin the foundation at Piacenza

Meanwhile, the day after the audience with the Holy Father Pius IX, I wanted to leave Rome at once, I did not want to see anything, only: «Let us go!» I said to my companion, but she would not hear of it because she liked seeing Rome, and then so many Bishops and Cardinals urged me to stay, saying that They would procure for me things for the chapel that I would open, and this was worse: every time they spoke to me of this I felt faint, and so too the dispensation to have the Most Blessed Sacrament, all in Pius IX's own hand.

Nothing served me as consolation, no, everything caused me pain. Finally it was decided to leave, after 28 days of suffering. I received so many gifts: chalices, pyxes, even the little bell, chasubles, the picture of St. Joseph, very beautiful, in the end they had to make crates and ship them by sea to Genoa. While we were traveling with this friend of mine and a Priest who had also found me in our same lodging, he came along with us and, since I was suffering greatly, they proposed to me to stop at Piacenza, where there were two very good souls whose acquaintance I would make. I let myself be persuaded and we stopped at a hotel, and shortly afterward these two priests of excellent spirit came and everything was told, what had happened to me and the reason for my going to Rome. These good souls, hearing this, begged me to begin the work at Piacenza, pointing out to me that it is a quiet city and that there was a good Bishop there, a great lover of good works, and that they would gladly lend themselves and would look for (an apartment). No sooner said than done: they took the trouble of looking provisionally for an apartment, so that afterward a palace would be bought, since there were so many for sale. I leave you to imagine how these plans hurt me; I always thought that time would still be needed, when, a few days after my arrival from Rome, I received a letter from these Priests in which they told me they had found the house very convenient and at a low price; they wanted a prompt reply. Armed with strength and my offering already made, I answered that they should fix it, that at the beginning of March I would come with other friends, and so it happened.

My God, how to say this to papa and mama and to the archbishop? for in giving him the account of the journey and of the audience I had said nothing at all about my stop at Piacenza because I did not have the courage; only that he comforted me and then said to me: «Well then, let us set to work.» What did I do: I sent things and everything that was needed without my parents knowing, because my small apartment was divided, that is, I had a free door; in agreement with the household staff I made the shipment and the first time that I left alone with the usual friend, they thought I was going to see the girl who was at school in Milan, but without saying anything I went to arrange as best I could the rooms that had been rented; I stayed there a few days and then returned and already had 5 friends of mine ready to follow me. I told the confessor everything I had done and he was a little [shaken] and he too feared for the relatives and the Archbishop. I took courage and told everything also to the archbishop, who did not want at all that I should have left Genoa, and told me that he did not give me his approval. My God, what to do? Meanwhile he said: «I accept no resignation of yours,» because I had many congregations. I begged him, but nothing. I spent most sorrowful days; the confessor also disapproved of the resolution I had taken. What did I do? thrown on the ground at the feet of my Crucifix: «Tell me, my Love, was this stopping at Piacenza your work or my illusion, and I let myself be deluded by those persons who advised me to do so? If I must not go, or however it be, speak to me and I shall carry out your commands, but take me out of so fierce a struggle, and make my archbishop consent and bless me.» A clear voice: «All my will what happened; be calm: everything will be smoothed over.» I needed nothing else and, after thanking my dear Crucifix, full of confidence I prepared for the departure. I returned to the archbishop and found him appeased and, with sorrow yes, but he blessed me; only he did not wish to accept resignations and told me that it was enough for me to return to Genoa every two months: the congregations would go on just the same. I was silent and promised that I would do so; then, [as for] the others that did not depend on the archbishop, I gave my resignation; they were new things, what I had to go through.

The beginnings of the Institute at Piacenza

At last I had my parents to persuade. Oh! how hard it was for me! I went through such a cruel agony; I cannot describe this event, I feel it! and yet without shedding a tear I told them. Oh! those two old people, what a scene! they kept an eye on me because they were afraid I would flee. At last the moment came: it was morning, the train left at 10; my friends were waiting for me at the station. Mama, having understood, sat down on the doorstep saying to me: «I shall see if you have the courage to pass me: you must step over me!» Papa was weeping, and never in my life had I seen him weep; all the others, it was heartbreaking. I took courage, gave a leap, stepped over mama and was outside. I took the stairs at a flight and straight to the station. So I began to feel in myself a lion's courage: nothing made an impression on me any more.

All having arrived at Piacenza, Oh! my Jesus, what I went through with those three. Two were bearable, and three... my Jesus, what terrible anguish! Meanwhile I looked for the house, always turning to the bishop to have a good lawyer, and I found one that seemed to me very suitable and began negotiations. The day before agreeing, that is, signing the contract, two friends of mine together with a priest, who had come from Genoa to visit me to spend two days with me, invited me to go with them, as they were going to visit a missionary, a certain Tornatore. They said to me: «Let us go and see him!» I agreed very willingly because he was said to be very ascetic... As soon as he saw us, he gave us a warm welcome and asked where we were and where we came from. The priest who was with us told him everything; as we left he said he would come to visit them.

The next day, just at the moment when I was with the lawyers making the contract, one of my two friends came and told me that both Priests were there, both Mr. Tornatore and the other, but I could not move, only when it came about that an addition had to be made to the contract; then, while the lawyers were writing, I left for a moment to greet them, who were about to leave, and I did not see him again. Everything having been done in order, we prepared to make the move, but how many pains!

There would be too much to say! A house that had nothing good but the exterior. Oh! what I did! but my God comforted me by assuring me that everything was permitted by Him. I had a giant's strength: the work, however heavy, and covered with penances, I felt nothing; at night I never went to bed: leaning on a table, an hour of sleep and to work, or lying on the floor on the platform in the Chapel, or on the cross and for a pillow an iron, that is a chain on which I laid my head, and then how much discipline! It was something. At last, not knowing where to go to confess, the desire came to me to go to Mr. Tornatore and the first times I liked it, but then it caused me a certain I-know-not-what of fear: his direction was so different from my former one. Enough, I cared little about it because my guide was my Jesus in everything and for everything.

Having arrived in the novena of the Immaculate, I asked the Bishop for a priest to give the holy exercises to those who would be clothed on the day of the Immaculate. He gave me Mr. Tornatore. The sisters were two of the first and three who had entered after we were already in the house we owned. He gave the holy Exercises and on the day of the Immaculate these 5 Sisters were clothed.

The name of the Institute: «Daughters of St. Anne»

Now I must go back to say how the name of St. Anne had already come and how the saint herself showed me the veil as it should be.

As soon as we arrived in this hovel, I looked for a small little room less badly kept to make the little Chapel, which the Bishop blessed and left the Lord in. Oh! how happy I felt to have my beloved with me and I spent whole nights there. Oh! what I did not have! One of these evenings, while I was alone, and prayed a great deal and in the very prayer felt such an intimate union with God, the little chapel is lit up by a great light and the Most Holy Virgin appeared to me and St. Anne and lower down, as if kneeling toward the Most Holy Virgin, St. Francis of Assisi. The Immaculate, distinctly, in a clear voice: «I desire that the title of the rules be Daughters of St. Anne my Mother (and here she pointed her out to me). I yield with great satisfaction to my Mother this Work. Do not be distressed: I shall always hold as done to me what you do for Her.» I remained in ecstasy and as soon as she said the last two words all three disappeared, and I kept seeming to see them and said nothing. In this way I stayed a long while, because having recovered I noticed that much time had passed. What to do? I kept thinking of the obligation to inform the Holy Father if the title had been given me, because the commandments were already printed with that title «Immaculate».

I could not find peace; I did not want anyone to know this; it was a great torment. Meanwhile I thought of letting the Holy Father know and through Cardinal Patrizi I sent him a writing of mine, and at once he ordered that they be so called and urged me to procure the regulation. This happened before the clothing and so they were called Daughters of St. Anne, and the oremus were made suitable for the clothing and later had modifications.

I make it my duty to send you what you commanded me the last time I had the grace to speak to you in person. Monastic Rules for the daughters of the Immaculate, the minims of St. Francis of Assisi. 1. Annual vow of chastity. 2. Vow of Obedience 3. Vow of poverty 4. Unmarried Daughters and widows will be admitted, who after a year of probation, if they have a vocation, the Superior will make professed. These shall devote themselves to the growth of our Holy Faith and to the assistance of the sick in their homes, and shall also receive with them endangered Girls, to whom they will teach Christian Doctrine and women's work. 5. To the sick persons whom they assist, if poor, they will bring something of necessity, and all will be free; from the rich they will accept an offering for the monastery. 6. 3. Extract from the Regulations of a new foundation under the title

of the Immaculate, the Minims of St. Francis of Assisi, Press

of the S.C. De Prop. Fide, Rome 1866; AFSA: B.2.75.

This text is an expansion of the First sketch; it was approved by the Bishop of Acqui in 1865, hence it is known in the Institute as the Regulations of Acqui; of this document we present only the Preface which sums up the purpose of the Institute: the exercise of a «noble, disinterested and gratuitous charity».

It was always a marvelous trait of Divine Providence to raise up, at the opportune time, Institutes best suited to the circumstances, the needs, the advantages of the Church and of souls. We do not think we stray far from the truth if we number among these loving dispositions of Divine Mercy the fact that in the present times it inspired the happy idea of an Association which, under the invocation and all-powerful patronage of the Blessed Virgin Mary Immaculate and of the Seraphic Patriarch of Assisi St. Francis, should devote itself first to its own Sanctification, then to that of others, through the exercise of a noble, disinterested and gratuitous Charity. At a time when, in order to destroy every supernatural idea, an attempt has been made to substitute for Christian Charity the sonorous but barren word Philanthropy, and everything transitory has been applauded as the glory of human progress, to the gravest detriment of what matters most, morality and religion, the love of Jesus Christ for the Church his spouse has inspired an institute that might serve as a counterpoint to the current ideas of the century and make known how powerful, even in the weaker sex, is charity toward God and neighbor, that charity which is an emanation of the Sacred Heart of Jesus for the benefit of the poor, the sick, all the suffering part which is so numerous in the human family.

The mere reading of the following rules of the new institute, and even a rapid examination of its aim and of the means to attain it, can show everyone the truth of what we have asserted.

Let due thanks therefore be rendered to Our Lord Jesus Christ who, in his infinite Mercy, and through the Intercession of his Immaculate Mother Mary Most Holy as well as of that saint who most distinguished himself in the exercise of Charity and in contempt of earthly things, willed to give a new pledge of his divine solicitude for the salvation of souls, and for the establishment, spread and prosperity of the new Institute let the most fervent prayers be raised to the Lord, to whom for all ages be Blessing, honor and Glory.

The principal aim of this Institute is to practice charity, of which the patroness Mary Most Holy and St. Francis of Assisi gave the supreme example.

b) Letter of the ven. G.B. Scalabrini

Most Rev. Eminence

In execution of the venerated orders that Your Most Rev. Eminence was pleased to communicate to me with your esteemed dispatch of 26 March of the current year no. 9773, I took care to gather in all secrecy the appropriate information on the relationship that once existed between the Foundress of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, Rosa Gattorno, widow Custo, and the Priest Fr. Luigi Cogrossi, now canon of that Basilica of S. Maria Regina Coeli of Monte Santo; from which information it results to me:

that the said Rosa Gattorno came to know Cogrossi from the year 1865, having seen him that year in Genoa, where she resided, and where he had gone; and she had also seen him at Castelleone, Diocese of Cremona, where Cogrossi was stationed, and where she had gone to visit him;

that Gattorno from then on, with the assent of Mgr. Charvaz, Archbishop of Genoa, of blessed memory, had confessed to Cogrossi, whom she still had as Confessor when about the middle of 1866 she came here to Piacenza to found her new Institute of Sister Nurses under the title of Minims of St. Francis of Assisi, which she then designated to be called Daughters of the Immaculate Conception and of St. Anne, and finally called simply Daughters of St. Anne;

that before the beginnings of this Institute and afterward, from the middle of 1866 until July 1867, Mrs. Rosa Gattorno made journeys in the company of Cogrossi from Genoa to Piacenza, and vice versa, to Rome and to other Cities with the sole intent, as her notorious virtues, above all censure, certainly lead one to suppose, of founding and promoting her Institute of Nurses, since even before she knew Cogrossi she had devoted herself in Genoa to the care of the sick.

It has also resulted to me that Cogrossi never had the spiritual direction of the House opened by Gattorno at Piacenza about the middle of 1866, as already said, in the manner of a Community, which was gradually forming and which therefore could not at once take precise and regular form;

that Cogrossi lived day and night, though in a separate apartment, in the same House until July 1867; at which time the Institute, which was beginning with rules not yet well established, had to undergo not only some variations but also internal contrarieties, of which Gattorno, as soon as she became aware, took the resolution to dismiss Cogrossi, who at the same time was deprived by my predecessor of the faculty to hear confessions in this Diocese.

It is also plausible that Gattorno left from here and arrived here at night in the town together with Cogrossi, taking into account the timetable of the Railway runs, which usually leave from here or arrive here at various hours of day and night.

I must besides add that, in the aforesaid Rosa Gattorno, because of the relationship she had with Cogrossi, none of the more sensible persons who came near her supposed there had been anything human, except in this: that she remained deluded by appearances, believing him for some time a servant of God, as she herself said to persons of confidence; and that is how she came to wish to confess to him.

Happy to have carried out, as best I was able, the orders of Your Most Rev. Eminence, and always ready for your wishes or commands, I prostrate myself to kiss the Sacred Purple, and I am honored to profess myself with all submission and veneration.

Of Your Most Rev. Eminence

Piacenza, 17 April 1878

Most devoted, most obedient servant

† GIOVANNI BATTISTA, Bishop of Piacenza To His Most Rev. Em.

13. Letter of Mgr. Antonio Ranza, bishop of Piacenza, dated 26 May 1871; ACDF: Gattorno Rosa.

The Bishop of Piacenza presents to the Prefect of the Congregation of BB. and RR. Rosa Gattorno, a Genoese woman come to Rome to submit to the Holy Congregation the Rules of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne; he bears witness to Gattorno's Christian piety, humility and zeal; the Daughters of St. Anne, spurred by the words and works of the foundress Gattorno, give proof of solid virtue and spirit of sacrifice and are a source of edification to the faithful.

Most Rev. Eminence

The exceptional goodness and kindness for which Your Most Rev. Eminence is so distinguished, and of which I have had innumerable proofs in the long course of years since you have presided over the Sacred Cong. of Bishops and Regulars, inspire in me courage and confidence to address to you this my letter of recommendation.

There is coming to that August City Mrs. Rosa Gattorno, Genoese by origin, about forty years of age, and a Widow for a long time, in order to submit to the examination of the aforementioned Sacred Cong. the Rules of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, which she longs to found and to see approved by the Apostolic Holy See.

Justice requires that I render praiseworthy testimony of the Christian piety, true humility and untiring zeal of which the same Lady has shown herself to be informed, who, though worn out in physical strength and subject to various ailments, does not cease to concern herself with and care for the two Houses opened in this City and two others opened in Genoa, her native city, and knows how to find a way to provide for their support.

The aim of such an Institute, which had its beginnings in this city of Piacenza about the middle of 1866, and which, although for about a year at the start it underwent some variations and contrarieties, even internal ones, nevertheless from 1867 onward has been acquiring greater stability and regularity, is to gather young women bound by simple vows and to offer them the means both of attending to their own sanctification by the practice of the Christian virtues and of the evangelical counsels, and of exercising themselves for the benefit of neighbor in the works of mercy, and especially in assisting the poor sick according to the norms laid down by the aforesaid Foundress, and also in the care of poor girls, either forsaken or in danger, whom they take in to instruct and educate according to the capacity of their age and condition.

I am pleased to attest that the young women, called Daughters of St. Anne, who already in a certain number have embraced such an Institute and conform to the Rules and to the spirit that the Foundress Gattorno dictates and instills in them by word and deed, give examples of solid virtue and of sacrifice in the various exercises of piety and mercy mentioned above, and in this way prove not only a source of edification to the faithful but also of benefit to the sick visited and assisted by them and to the girls housed in their Houses.

Wherefore I judge it my duty to recommend the petitioner Rosa Gattorno to Your Most Rev. Eminence, that you may deign to help her with light and direction, favoring her as much as you can with your good offices with the Most Eminent Fathers and His Holiness, from Whom she invokes a special blessing for herself and for her Institute.

Allow me to ask your pardon for the inconvenience I cause You, and grant me the grace of prostrating myself to kiss the Sacred Purple and of professing myself with full esteem and submission.

Of Your Most Rev. Eminence

Piacenza, 26 May 1871

Anna Maria Rosa Gattorno of Genoa, come to Ferrara with ten Sisters dependent on her, called there by the Pious Lady Mrs. Princess Donna Marianna Pallavicini - Countess widow Trotti to open a House there, for which purpose the praised Lady acquired a grand Palace which she is having restored at her own expense, not without great outlay, and has also assured them for a certain time their sustenance, so that they might work especially for the benefit of the poor class. Indeed, as soon as the Schools were opened they became numerous, with some hundreds of girls, cultivated, as is reported to me, most edifyingly in religion, in piety, and in women's work, while the Members who make up the Family do not fail to go, always in twos, to the care of the Sick of whatever condition and sex in their homes, and I hear that their work in this respect too proves most welcome, occupying themselves with holy zeal in disposing the sick to receive the Sacraments. The Superior then, toward the end of the same month of October, returned to Piacenza, where the Mother House exists with a numerous band of Orphan girls whom that Municipality has entrusted to this Institute. There too is found the Spiritual Director, who is believed to be the author of the Rules. This Institute has spread to other Dioceses, and I believe that recently the Superior opened a sixth House at Nice.

For the rest, through some upright Ecclesiastic an effort will be made in Ferrara to investigate their spirit, piety and conduct better; but the Holy Congregation can be better informed by the Ecclesiastical Authority of Piacenza, where the Institute arose. As for the Foundress, she shows in truth a docile and pious spirit, disposed to whatever resolution the Holy See might take concerning her Institute, as also to receive the Rule that will be presented to her, wherefore it will be prudent to carry out the withdrawal of the repeated printings without publicity, through the Ordinaries.

This is what I can signify for the moment, the occasion being favorable to reaffirm myself with the most profound respect, most humbly kissing your hands. Of Your Eminence.

Rome, from the Apostolic Dataria, 17 February 1872

Most humble, devoted Servant

Decretum

Rosa Gattorno, of the diocese of Genoa, in the year 1866, in the city of Piacenza, laid the foundations of a Society of pious women, whom she willed to be called daughters of St. Anne, Mother of the Virgin Mary Immaculate, and she determined that they should apply themselves above all to this: that, having made profession of the simple Vows of poverty, obedience and chastity, they devote themselves to their own and others' sanctification, to the pious and religious instruction of girls, especially if they are poor, and to the help and relief of the sick. This pious Society was in a short time enlarged and extended, to the great benefit of the Christian faithful. Most recently the same Foundress, who also exercises the office of Superior General, earnestly petitioned Our Most Holy Lord Pope Pius IX to deign to approve the aforesaid pious Society and its Constitutions, of which she presented a copy, with the support of the Prelates of the places in which the pious Society is found. But His Holiness, in the Audience held by the undersigned Lord Secretary of this Sacred Congregation of Bishops and Regulars on the 31st of March of the Year 1876, having regard to the Letters of Recommendation of the aforementioned Prelates, in most ample words praised and commended the said pious Society as an Institute of simple Vows under the government of a Superior General, saving the jurisdiction of the Ordinaries according to the form of the Sacred Canons and the Apostolic Constitutions, as by the tenor of the present Decree he praises and commends it, the approval of the pious Society and of the Constitutions being deferred to a more opportune time, concerning which in the meantime he ordered some observations to be communicated. Let the Sisters of the said Society continue unceasingly to apply themselves to procuring their own and others' sanctification and, above all, with every effort and labor to teach young girls the fear of the Lord, to imbue them with good and holy morals, to arouse them to the love of the Catholic Religion, and also to exercise assiduously and promptly works of charity toward the sick, especially the poor, so as to answer the wishes of the Supreme Pontiff, to whom nothing is more desirable than that, in these most turbulent times, provision be made for the education of Catholic youth and help and relief be brought to the wretched. Given at Rome, from the Secretariat of the Sacred Congregation of Bishops and Regulars, on 8 April 1876.

I. Card. FERRIERI

C - DOCUMENTS RELATING TO THE RULES

The Servant of God had the overall intuition of the Institute to be founded; the Rules, on the other hand, were written by Fr. Giovanni Battista Tornatore CM, in agreement with the Foundress, and had a rather long iter.

In 1867 the Servant of God turned to Tornatore so that he would write the

°

Rules.

At the beginning of February 1868 the work Words of the glorious St. Anne mother of the Immaculate who presents the Rules to her daughters was praised by the bishop of Piacenza Mgr. Antonio Ranza (cf. infra no. 1), after examination by a commission of theologians appointed by the Bishop himself (Letter of Fr. Tornatore to the ven. G.B. Scalabrini, dated 6 April 1877).

On 17 July 1868 the Servant of God sent the Holy Father the rules in manuscript and asked for approval (cf. infra no. 2).

Obtaining no reply, she presented the Rules again, this time printed, in May 1871, together with another small volume, also written by Fr. Tornatore: Application of the Common Rules to the sister nurses.

The consultors' vote was negative and in August 1871 the booklets were passed to the Holy Office, without the Servant of God being informed.

By a letter dated 20 January 1872 the Holy Office ordered that the copies of the Rules be withdrawn and burned and that the Author be removed from the Institute, but no mention was made of the reasons for the measure.

The Servant of God, who had greatly praised the Rule to the sisters, showed a heroic obedience (cf. infra no. 4) that aroused the admiration even of Card. Vannicelli, who praised the sisters for their «prompt obedience without resentment» (Letter of 19 March 1872).

The Servant of God was ordered to draw up a Draft of Constitutions under the guidance of Mgr. Giordani, auxiliary in Ferrara of Card. Vannicelli (Letter of 6 March 1872). In contradiction with the severe measures taken, she was ordered to derive the new rules from the observance (Letter of 21 April 1872: until that moment the sisters had observed the condemned rule!) and it was suggested to her that the first rules could be kept for explanation.

In June 1872 the Draft of Constitutions written by the Servant of God was sent to the Congregation of BB. and RR. (Letter of Card. Vannicelli dated 14 June 1872) and in December the Congregation transmitted it to Fr. Leonardo Fava SJ for a reworking (Letter of the Servant of God to the Congregation of BB. and RR. dated 16 December 1872).

In March 1873 the Servant of God asked that two other consultors be placed alongside Fr. Fava and expressed the strong fear that a new spirit would be given to the Constitutions (cf. infra no. 6).

On 4 April 1873 the text of Constitutions given to Fr. Fava was withdrawn and returned to the Congregation of BB. and RR. The Servant of God asked that they have the kindness to hear her (cf. infra no. 7).

On the proposal of the Secretary of the Congregation of BB. and RR. and at the Foundress's insistence, the consultor Fr. Raimondo Bianchi OP drew up a new sketch of Constitutions, but when the work was finished the Servant of God did not accept it because it did not answer the needs of the Institute (Vote of Fr. Bianchi dated 15 February 1876).

In 1874 a text of Constitutions was printed with the approval ad experimentum of Card. Vannicelli, Protector of the Institute. The Author is without doubt Fr. Tornatore.

At the beginning of 1876 a new text of Constitutions in manuscript was presented to the Congregation of BB. and RR., in the hand of Fr. Tornatore, who wrote it by order of Card. Giuseppe Berardi, new Protector of the Institute (cf. Summ., p. 803). Shortly afterward the Institute received the Decree of praise.

p. 752

.

This text of the Constitutions, finally accepted by the Congregation of BB. and RR., underwent successive modifications: in 1876, 1879, 1881, 1884. In 1885 it was approved ad experimentum for ten years.

After further modifications it was definitively approved on 26 July 1892.

EPISCOPATE OF PIACENZA

Most Eminent Prince

May Your Most Rev. Eminence deign to receive, with your accustomed kindness, what I come to set before you.

There is perhaps no Institute that is now spreading in the Church so greatly as that of the Daughters of St. Anne. It counts barely a few years of life and already about sixty Houses have been founded by it in Italy. Providence, moreover, seems to wish to open a new road for it, since, within the current month, several nuns of this Institute will depart for the City of La Paz in Bolivia, with the aim of erecting there also two new Houses, in accordance with the desire and prayers of the President of that Republic, of the Bishop of the said City and of various other distinguished Personages. Most numerous, finally, are the applications that from day to day are submitted, by girls of the countryside and of the people especially, to be admitted to belong to an Institute so suited to them, and in fact they enter it in great numbers.

All this makes me keenly desire that the rules be approved by the Holy See as soon as possible, since only then will there be uniform, invariable and constant discipline in all the Houses, both of Italy and abroad. In this way, moreover, the Superior General will be in part relieved of the heavy burden that she is now obliged to bear; nor will I conceal from You, Most Eminent Prince, that my own action too would then acquire far more effectiveness, being able to require the observance of fixed, untouchable and sure rules, rules that must direct the postulancy and novitiate of the aspirants and everything that pertains to the General House existing in Piacenza.

I know the exceptional prudence and the extraordinary circumspection that the Holy See uses, and deservedly, in such matters; nevertheless I dare to beg You, Most Eminent Prince, as much as I know and can, that my request be granted. It is not fitting that a Congregation of nuns, which now counts more than five hundred persons, be left at the mercy of a single person, be she ever so sensible and pious.

It is dear to me at the same time to be able to assure Your Most Rev. Eminence that this Congregation truly does very great good. There may indeed be defects in it, like all human things, but they will disappear once the approved rules are put into effect. Even where conflicts arose things quieted down, and Mgr. Archbishop of Florence was at last persuaded that they were mere calumnies and, writing to the Superior, gave fine testimony to the virtues of the Daughters of St. Anne, and hopes very well of them.

With the most profound respect I kiss the sacred Purple, having the high honor of professing myself of Your Most Rev. Eminence.

Most devoted, most obsequious servant

† GIOVANNI BATTISTA, Bishop of Piacenza

The text of the Constitutions definitively approved in 1892, as regards the spiritual and charismatic part, is distinguished by a single notable difference from the first text presented in 1876: the article On the aim of the Institute.

The article of 1876 has the merit of recalling the Daughters of St. Anne to the vocation to holiness common to all Christians and of indicating in the Institute's reference to St. Anne mother of the Immaculate a not secondary component of the charism.

The article of 1892, anticipating the Secundum quas norms that would be issued some years later, speaks of «primary end and secondary end» of the Institute; it makes no reference to St. Anne nor to the universal vocation to holiness and therefore represents a doctrinal impoverishment. The modification of the article is due to the Consultors of the Congregation of BB. and RR., as appears from the corrections that show in the text existing in the Archive of the Congregation for Religious and Secular Institutes (P 31).

a) Constitutions of the Daughters of St. Anne Mother of the Immaculate (1876).

Chapter 1 of the Institute

Article 1 on the aim of the Institute

The end that the Daughters of St. Anne have in common with all Christians is to imitate Jesus Christ, author and model of all holiness, sanctifying themselves, and cooperating, to the extent they can, in the sanctification of their neighbor; and to honor the prerogatives of their holy mother, above all that of being mother of the Virgin Immaculate.

They will cooperate in the sanctification of their neighbor by practicing toward him the following acts of charity and mercy: 1st assistance to the sick in their homes and in hospitals, whatever the condition, the sex, the illness of the sick; to men, however, they will render only those services permitted by the most reserved modesty; 2nd education of girls, especially of those who are in danger of being lost; 3rd school for girls of the poor class; 4th school and Christian doctrine for little boys from seven to ten years.

This end is like the badge that distinguishes the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne from all those planted in the garden of Holy Church.

Chapter I

ON THE END OF THE INSTITUTE

The Institute of the daughters of St. Anne proposes above all the personal sanctification of its own members, to whom it offers all the means to progress in perfection, the aim of the religious state. It has then as secondary end works of zeal and mercy, devoting itself:

1st. To the care of the sick in their homes and in hospitals, whatever their condition, sex or illness.

2nd. To the education of girls, especially those who are in danger of being lost.

3rd. To the school for girls, especially of the poor class, to infant Asylums and Asylums for the incurable.

Chapter II

ON SUITABLE CANDIDATES FOR THE INSTITUTE

There may be admitted to this Institute unmarried women who, having given unequivocal signs of vocation, have reached the fifteenth year of age and not passed the twenty-fifth.

For the illegitimate, widows, and those over twenty-five years, a dispensation of the Holy See is necessary. It is further required that, besides the certificates of Baptism, Confirmation, and of free status, the aspirants have such an attestation of good conduct as places their reputation above every suspicion.

Chapter III

ON THE MEANS IN GENERAL EMPLOYED BY THE INSTITUTE

TO ATTAIN ITS END

In order that the Institute may succeed in attaining its end, it must employ all its forces in clothing itself with the spirit of Jesus Christ, which shines forth principally in his poverty, chastity and obedience, in his regular observance, in the exercises of piety, in the practice of the virtues, especially of charity toward neighbor, of meekness and humility, of simplicity and prudence, of modesty, of detachment from relatives.

Now of all these means and of each in particular something will be said in the following chapter.

Chapter IV

TO ATTAIN ITS END

Article I

On the three vows of Poverty, Chastity and Obedience

Postulants, after three months of trial, or more in those cases in which the Mother General and her council judge it necessary to prolong the probation, will be admitted to the clothing, preceded by a set of spiritual exercises.

The Novitiate lasts two years. In the first year the apostolic decrees and Constitutions concerning the Novitiate will be rigorously observed, nor may the Novices be occupied in the works proper to the Institute. In the second year the Novitiate will be less rigorous, and the Novices may therefore be exercised also in these works. At the end of the two years of the Novitiate, and the Ordinary having ascertained the will of the Novices, and a course of spiritual exercises having again been made, they will be admitted to the three simple annual vows of poverty, chastity and obedience.

After ten years of temporary profession the Sisters will make the perpetual simple vows.
