§ 1 - On the vow of Poverty

The Professed may retain the radical ownership of their own goods; but the administration of them and the disbursement of the income arising from them is wholly forbidden to them. Therefore before profession they must cede the administration, use and usufruct of the said goods to whomever they please, and also to the Institute, if they so wish. This cession may also be made by private act and the condition may be attached that it be always and at any time revocable. The professed sister, however, will not make use of this reservation without Apostolic approval.

The above shall hold and be observed also for those goods that may come to the sisters by inheritance or by any other legitimate title after profession.

They may then dispose of the ownership of all the goods mentioned above, either by will or, with prior license of the Superior General, by act between living persons; and in this second case the cession of administration, use and usufruct made as above will lapse, provided, however, that the sister disposing of the ownership does not wish the said cession to last for the longer time that she may please, notwithstanding the disposition of the ownership.

Moreover, the professed are not forbidden to perform, on the goods of which they retain the radical ownership, those acts that are prescribed by the laws, having first asked the license of the Superior General. Of all that the Sisters acquire by their own industry, or that

is given to them in consideration of the Institute, they may appropriate nothing, but it must go entirely to the benefit of the Institute itself.

By the simple vow of poverty, the daughters of St. Anne may not turn to their own use anything of the common goods of the Institute without license of the Superior.

It belongs to her to distribute to each according to need clothing, books, and furnishings; and without her permission none may do or give away anything of the house.

Since the things of the house must all be without luxury and wealth, but conformed to poverty, so out of love for this virtue the Sisters will be content that the most lowly and least good things be given to them. They will be ready to leave the things given for their use at the slightest sign from the Superior.

They will not keep anything locked with a key, not even the room, without license of the Superior; who may every three months, or even more often, change the rooms and whatever belongs to them.

The Sisters must be careful that through their negligence what they have for their use or for their own office is neither lost nor worn out. If they mislay or break anything, let them notify the Superior; and if they find anything lost, let them bring it to her. When they change house, apart from their clothes, they must take nothing with them of what is granted for their use, without the license of the Superior.

And in case a sister should leave the Institute, the latter will have the right to claim one lira a day for the time she remained in the probation and in the first year of Novitiate, plus one hundred fifty lire to cover the expenses of the Clothing.

'

The dowry of the postulants will be one thousand lire. It may not be reduced or remitted without license of the Holy See.

The dowry will be invested securely, and should a Sister leave the Institute it will be returned to her without interest, but with the deductions mentioned above.

§ 2 - On the vow of Chastity

By the simple vow of chastity the daughters of St. Anne consecrate spirit and body to God. Therefore by virtue of this vow they bind themselves especially to abstain from all immodest acts, internal and external, that are forbidden to the faithful by the sixth and ninth precept of the Decalogue, so that the violation of this obligation would be for them a sacrilege.

To keep this vow perfectly, the sisters must keep the mind occupied with the thought of Jesus Christ, of the Most Holy Mother and of the Saints. They must keep guarded the external senses, the eyes, hearing, touch. Not rest outside the permitted time, never be idle.

They must mortify gluttony, not eating or drinking outside the customary times, without the license of the Superior.

In writing or speaking to persons of the other sex, let them not use affectionate words, even if they are pious persons; let them not speak with them at times and places not permitted, nor come too near them, nor let the presence of some sister designated by the Superior ever be lacking, as will be said below. In assisting the sick, whether in Hospitals or at home, let them have a holy fear of doctors, surgeons, attendants etc.

When of necessity they must speak with them, let the demeanor be wholly religious and have nothing worldly. Let them never permit themselves to be touched, and reject at all costs any act, even the smallest, of the like kind. If a sister observes that another in such a case failed, let her inform the Superior.

Those who teach girls must refrain from forming a particular friendship with any of them.

In all circumstances in which they must deal with neighbor, let their reserve be so great that not even the malicious may have a pretext to form suspicions contrary to their perfect chastity and modesty. Even when conversing among themselves they must guard against too much familiarity and particular friendship; allow themselves no free act, avoid embraces or anything else that might even slightly offend holy purity, and let them all regard one another with the greatest respect as true spouses of Jesus Christ, who is purity by essence.

§ 3 - On the vow of Obedience

By the simple vow of obedience the daughters of St. Anne renounce their own will, abandoning for the love of God all of themselves and their things into the hands of the Superior, to obey her according to the letter and spirit of the constitutions. But to point out some particular cases: none will give or send in writing anything whatever without license of the Superior; none will correct a sister for the faults she may have observed in her, if she is not deputed to this by the Superior or by her own office. This is understood if charity did not require otherwise. None will enter another's room without license of the Superior; and when such license is had, for all the time they remain together the door will be open.

None will take food outside the customary times or outside the house without the license of the Superior. None may refuse the office entrusted to her by the Superior, or abandon it without her permission. None may perform penances beyond the common ones without license of the Superior. None may disclose the matters of her spirit to another sister, and much less to an outside person, except the Confessor, without the license of the Superior. If one has received a refusal from the immediate Superior, she will not have recourse to the Superior General without disclosing to her the refusal received and its motive, if she knows it. The Superior reads the letters written or received by the members of her Community. Excepted, however, are letters coming from the Holy See, the Ordinary, and the Superior General, or addressed to these by the Sisters. Let them be well persuaded that the Superior holds for them the place of the Lord, and that by obeying her they obey God himself. Consequently they will obey her with a cheerful and persevering obedience in all things in which there is no sin.

Let them try to be ready at the sound of the bell that calls to the common acts, leaving in this case even a letter unfinished if they are occupied in writing.

Article IV

On the practice of the virtues

§ 1 - On the theological virtues

The daughters of St. Anne must first of all be well persuaded that the words of Jesus Christ are infallible, and that by conforming their works to them they will arrive in Heaven to see Him himself who is the eternal and infinite truth.

p. 767

Let them ask the grace to be always united to the infallible head of the Church, the Supreme Pontiff, from whom the doctrine of Jesus Christ is always had.

Besides this, they must seek in God and in his grace that spring of living water which can make them blessed for eternity, and to obtain it let them ask the Lord for the help and strength always to observe his law and the constitutions of their own Institute. Let them ask the grace to be ready to endure any suffering and death itself rather than offend their Divine Master, living like little children in his arms, sure that nothing will be lacking to them of what is necessary to make them wholly his, and nothing will happen that can prevent it, if they wish, of loving and enjoying him forever.

§ 2 - On simplicity and prudence

The daughters of St. Anne, mindful of that saying of Our Lord — Be simple as doves and prudent as serpents — will exercise the virtue of simplicity with God, with their Superiors, and with neighbor, seeing to it that their words are the sincere expression of their thoughts, their actions witnesses of their intention, their exterior in full accord with their spirit, and that none be deceived by them. Moreover they will seek in all their steps to be enlightened to discover where the divine will lies, the will of their Constitutions, that of their Superiors, in order to embrace it; where the true good of their neighbor lies, in order to procure it for him to the measure of their strength; where their own evil lies, in order to avoid it. By so doing they will be truly simple and prudent, that is, such as Jesus Christ Our Lord wants them.

§ 3 - On meekness and humility

Learn from me, says the Lord, for I am meek and humble of heart. The daughters of St. Anne will show that they have learned this most important lesson well from Him if, without complaints and with a cheerful face, they bear all the injuries done to them, especially in dealing with the sick whom they serve, and with the girls whom they teach; if, sincerely confessing their wretchedness, they hold it dear that their faults be known to their superiors, to be warned by them to amend them; if they shun praises, if they gladly embrace reproaches, persecutions and crosses. Let them be persuaded that the exercise of these virtues will make them acquire peace of heart, the affection of neighbor and eternal beatitude.

§ 4 - On modesty and cleanliness

Let the daughters of St. Anne be careful that in their bearing there be nothing disordered, nothing distracted in the eyes, especially in Church, at table, and in all public actions, nothing soft and studied in speaking, nothing childish in gesturing, nothing affected in walking.

Let them not be sordid in their clothing; let them, however, guard against too much neatness: let them not leave the room unless dressed in the whole habit: let them not touch one another either through levity or in play.

§ 5 - On detachment from relatives

The daughters of St. Anne will receive the visits of relatives in the company of a sister assigned by the superior, who will not leave until the visit is over. The visit of father and mother is excepted, which is received without a companion.

Let these visits of relatives be rare, nor let them write to them too often.

Let the sisters neither ask nor receive anything from relatives, and give them nothing without the license of the Superior.

When they write to relatives let them not enter into family affairs, such as marriages, lawsuits, jobs. If there were a necessity for such things let them consult the Superior.

In their conversations with their fellow sisters let them refrain from bringing in what touches their relatives. Let them guard against the desire to be assigned to a house near their relatives and their homeland.

Let them not make to outside persons recommendations of their relatives, even very needy ones, without the license of the Superior.

Let them not go to the house of their relatives or parents, even in case of illness and death, without the license of the Superior General.

p. 769

§ 6 - On the exact observance of the constitutions

The daughters of St. Anne will attain the fullness of the spirit of their vocation by observing their Constitutions, since in them they have a sure means that leads them to the observance of the commandments of God and of the Church, and to the practice of the evangelical counsels, in which consists all the holiness of the Christian.

To succeed in observing them they will use the following practices. In the morning, putting on the habit, they will kiss it as a sign of affection for their vocation. Every three months they will read them in common. It is not permitted to give them to anyone to read without the express license of the General.

§ 7 - On right intention

The daughters of St. Anne must be persuaded that the holy actions they perform for the benefit of neighbor will not be fully pleasing to the Lord, unless they do them principally for the motive of pleasing Him and glorifying Him.

Means to succeed well in this are: to guard against human respect, and not to seek one's own satisfaction. Therefore let them be careful to repress the vain complacency that arises from seeing one's own work pleasing and also praised by creatures, thinking of those words that Christ will say to the vainglorious: — You have received your reward. — Let them not be dejected to the point of losing peace, if their work were disapproved and censured. In this case let them think that Our Lord Jesus Christ, although he did everything well, was yet so many times censured and condemned. Let them glorify God by confessing from the heart their own nothingness, and remain in peace. Let them guard, however, against that foolish and false humility that makes one work with negligence for fear of praise and vainglory.

Another means of perfection will be to repress at once the first stirrings of envy that might be felt against those Institutes which, having similar functions, were praised and approved and prospered more than one's own. And if they truly love the glory of the Lord they will rejoice in the good that other Institutes do and will pray God to make them prosper.

Another means will be to flee bitter zeal, which would make them harsh toward themselves and toward the persons entrusted to their care. To abandon oneself to this false zeal is a sign that in faults the offense to God does not displease, and in virtue the glory of God does not please; but in the former one's own confusion displeases, and in the latter one's own glory and honor please.

D - RELATIONS OF THE SERVANT OF GOD

WITH THE BARBIELLINI FAMILY

The complexity of the Servant of God's human story, her condition as mother of a family and as foundress of a religious family, caused her in some cases to be the target of diametrically opposed accusations: according to some, she would have neglected her natural family to favor the sisters; according to others, she would have kept the sisters in straitened circumstances to favor her relatives. The testimonies at the Process (Summ., first part) largely answer these accusations; nevertheless, as a duty of justice, we report some of the numerous documents that show the heroic fortitude exercised by the Servant of God toward her relatives.

p. 771

The Servant of God was bound by tender affection to all her family members, on whom she always lavished her care with great generosity and sacrifice, especially in case of illness, as happened with her paternal grandmother, her sister Giustina (Memoirs of Francesco Gattorno, 1901) and in particular her husband: in this case she aroused the admiration even of the priests, as appears from the death certificate of Gerolamo Custo (cf. Summ., p. 699).

Particularly lively and affectionate was her relationship with her children: Francesco, who died at a few months of age, Carlotta, who became deaf-mute at a tender age, and Alessandro. They, grown up, repaid their mother with great affection, but were the cause of great sorrows to the Servant of God, especially Carlotta because of her marriage.

In 1876 Carlotta married Count Gaspare Barbiellini Amidei. With the dowry contract stipulated before the wedding, the Servant of God undertook to pay her daughter a dowry of L. 80,000 (cf. infra no. 1) and fulfilled the commitment ten years later with the purchase of an estate in the Piacenza countryside; Count Barbiellini, besides the noble title, owned nothing. The couple settled in Piacenza in a house adjoining the Mother House, since Carlotta could not be far from mama and had continual recourse to her, given her condition as a deaf-mute.

At the beginning it seemed a happy marriage, and it was, at least on Carlotta's part. Gaspare showed himself very pious, approached the Sacraments frequently and won the esteem and trust of his mother-in-law and of the sisters. In 1877 the Servant of God appointed him her general procurator and made use of him for many affairs of the Institute. Very soon, however, Barbiellini showed a great greed for money, so much as to suggest that the reason for the marriage was, for him, economic interest (cf. infra no. 9).

Between 1882 and 1886, during the construction of the generalate house in Rome, an adjoining plot was bought with money of the Gattorno family and a small villa was built, owned partly by the children of the Servant of God and partly by Federico Gattorno, brother of the Servant of God. This house had no communication with the sisters' house.

In 1884 Barbiellini was charged by the Servant of God to oversee the enlargement works of the Mother House in Piacenza, and he took advantage of it not only to have works carried out at the same time in his own dwelling (it was common talk in the city that he fraudulently had the sisters pay his own bills) but also to have the payment receipts issued in his own name, as if the money he used were not the Servant of God's (AFSA: Foundations: Piacenza Mother House - Works 1884-1899). In 1889 he claimed reimbursement of these alleged expenses, asking the Servant of God to pay a debt of his to Marianna Bertola of L. 20,000; the Servant of God flatly refused, whereupon, to spare her further sorrows, Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega (in the world Marchioness Anna Carrega) settled it with her own money.

From 1876 to 1884 between the Mother House and the Barbiellini house in Piacenza there was no other internal communication apart from a rustic door between the two gardens (cf. infra no. 2). In 1884, during the enlargement works, an internal communication was opened between the two houses by means of a corridor. The door, however, could not be opened arbitrarily by one side alone, since a key was needed on the Mother House side and one on the Barbiellini side. The key on the Mother House side was kept by the cook, who controlled the entry and exit of the Barbiellini (cf. Summ., p. 622).

From 1891 to 1894 the Servant of God charged Barbiellini with the administration of the Gargatano estate (Piacenza), a charge that Barbiellini desired and asked for insistently.

In 1895 Barbiellini presented to the Servant of God two payment demands of L. 106,400 and L. 151,500 (cf. infra nos. 4 and 5) and, to force her to pay, left his wife Carlotta with the children in the Mother House, threatening to leave forever if she did not satisfy him. The matter was put into the hands of the lawyer Giancarlo Bonfiglio (Memorial of the lawyer Bonfiglio; cf. infra no. 8), but Barbiellini, after having tried to corrupt him, would not deal with him. Two arbitrators were then appointed to settle the dispute: Federico Gattorno and Fr. Luigi da Sezze OFM Cap. (in the world Carlo Mercuri), who decided that, taking into account only the management of Gargatano, Barbiellini should be paid the sum of L. 18,507.42 (cf. infra no. 7); according to the opinion of the lawyer Bonfiglio, on the contrary, Barbiellini was a debtor to the Institute and would have been so recognized by a civil court, but Barbiellini evidently counted on the fact that his mother-in-law, a religious and Foundress, would never bring members of her own family before a civil court.

In 1896 the Servant of God revoked from Barbiellini the general power of attorney made in 1877 (cf. infra no. 10), something she had been thinking of doing for at least two years (cf. infra no. 3).

In 1899 Maria Adelaide Barbiellini, granddaughter of the Servant of God, succeeded in wheedling from her grandmother a sheet signed in blank, but the Servant of God, shortly before her death, annulled it by legal act, protecting the Institute from future claims (cf. infra no. 13).

After the death of the Servant of God, which occurred on 6 May 1900, Barbiellini continued to advance economic claims against the Institute.

In June 1900 he denounced Sr. A. Giuseppa Troni, superior of the Mother House, of having stolen documents from his dwelling in Piacenza. The following year the Court of Piacenza not only acquitted Troni of every accusation, but

p. 773

defined Barbiellini as an «exploiter» who «deserves no credence» (cf. infra no. 14).

In July 1900 he provoked a lawsuit before the Court of Rome, claiming that the Servant of God had not settled an alleged expense for jewels (Fracassini case; the case was not carried to completion).

In 1901 Carlotta Custo turned to the Holy Father accusing the Sisters of having removed gold objects and valuables from the room of the Servant of God at her death, things that belonged to her. In reality a locked box belonging to Carlotta had been handed over to the owner in May 1900 in the presence of two witnesses.

In 1906 Barbiellini provoked two further lawsuits before the civil Courts and pursued them for six years. In 1912 the Institute, though having won both cases, undertook to pay an annual pension to the daughter of the Servant of God for the rest of her natural life. Carlotta died in 1926.

8. Declaration of the lawyer Giancarlo Bonfiglio, dated 1 June 1901; AFSA: Judicial cases Custo, Miscellaneous.

The lawyer has been informed of Count Barbiellini's claims against the Institute; he therefore informs the Superior General of the Daughters of St. Anne about the events of which he was a witness during the life of the Servant of God and demonstrates in a clear and unequivocal way Barbiellini's wrongs.

Most Reverend Mother

The fact that I have just had to learn from the communications made to me by You — namely that Count Gaspare Barbiellini has set about submitting a petition to the Supreme Ecclesiastical Authority, to obtain the condemnation of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne to pay him huge sums by way of restitution and indemnity — did not surprise me at all, because I knew very well that he, being unable to entertain any hope of obtaining such a measure from the civil authority, would have to cling to the present course, perhaps in the hope that the fear of seeing the name of the Institute given as food to public curiosity might induce the Ecclesiastical Authority to impose a settlement, in which, as already happened another time, he, who is creditor of nothing, could not but end by gaining something.

I so foresaw what has now happened that, in 1895 — and on the occasion when I was charged by the unforgettable Mother Gattorno to settle every relation with Count Barbiellini, and thus had occasion to be able to weigh his reasons and appreciate his conduct — I thought it useful to draw up a documented memorial, from which the Daughters of St. Anne might draw their future defenses.

At that time I had to persuade myself that no reason of justice or equity assisted him — and that his tactic would consist in presenting a nucleus of demands, ready not to insist on the greater part of them, provided something were given him to silence the others — thus succeeding little by little, by presenting them again afterward and repeating the same game, in obtaining what absolutely did not belong to him.

On the basis of this sure conviction of mine — and having a conciliatory mandate — I spoke to him plainly, and while I was certain that nothing was due to him for the questions concerning the building of the Novitiate, the Dowry of his wife and the indemnity for administration, and that, as regards the administration of Gargatano, he was instead in debt, both by his own accounts, in which the greater part of the items were not justified, and by the fact of evident malversations, I nevertheless offered him a sum of 10 thousand lire and more — provided he would settle definitively on all the questions.

He saw himself found out and, falsifying the facts and artificially creating misunderstandings (see my memorial of that time), arranged to break off every negotiation with me (as you had broken off with the prince of Fitalia, when he had hoped that I was corruptible), waiting for better fortune from whoever might be charged in my place, on the next occasion.

And he did not miss. Mother Gattorno, weary of the continual battling, in which the Count's chief weapon (it is well not to forget it, and You, Most Reverend Mother, know it better than I) consisted in provoking, by suggestions and ill-treatment, the nervous crises of his own wife and in inciting his own children, not excluding the smallest, against their grandmother, in the spring of 1896 let herself be induced to accept the Count's tactic and to appoint two arbitrators to settle the Gargatano matter alone. These, certainly persuaded that they were doing a work of mercy, and perhaps ignorant of the true state of things — taking as basis only the accounts presented by Barbiellini, and evidently neglecting the examination of the documents (which could not be different from those presented to me in August 1895 and which left the Count in debt) — liquidated for him a credit of L. 13,007.42, which was punctually paid — and in which was included also the indemnity for Administration, which was absolutely not due.

Evidently his tactic was the good one.

What does he ask now?

Certainly not a supplement to the dowry — because the dowry of 80,000 lire was punctually paid to him with the property at Podenzano — and because in this the Institute would have nothing to do.

Certainly not an indemnity for the Administration of Gargatano because this, as has been seen, was already liquidated to him by the arbitrators and, unfortunately, paid by the Institute. He cannot evidently (given that since 1895 he had no more charges from the Mother and it is to be supposed that, being already in such enormous outlay then, she made him no more other largesse or loans!) have set about asking anything but what he asked in 1895, reduced by what referred to Gargatano and which was, unfortunately, already liquidated, and by the dowry.

Then he asked an indemnity of L. 54,000 for his work as procurator from 1876 to 1894. Lire 13,000 as outlay made in the building of the novitiate — with L. 9,100 interest on that sum — Lire 6,900 for works done by the nuns in the convent, not paid by them and paid instead by him. Lire 10,000 for having worked on the Mother's cases and procured documents. L. 8,000 because the nuns of Sampierdarena lived for 4 years in the Mother's house on which was the mortgage granted as guarantee of her daughter's dowry — and finally Lire 5,400 because the nuns had for three years the keys of the house in Via Merulana belonging to the Count.

And so in total Lire 106,400.

But the reasons for which his credit then ought not to subsist have not disappeared now; rather they have been reinforced.

I

The lire 54,000 thousand of indemnity as procurator were not and are not due.

Barbiellini says that L. 3,000 of annual indemnity were promised to him.

p. 786

Mother Gattorno always assured me that she never promised them (and the why we shall see below), and if documents were brought forward they would be either false documents or papers bearing some signature of the Mother, arbitrarily filled in.

Secondly, the mandate is always gratuitous when the contrary is not agreed — and this by law.

In the third place it is certain that while the Count's work was always harmful, at times unspeakable (See Veneziani Deposition, Annex B), Mother Gattorno always thought of maintaining him and his family in a very lordly manner, and such that three thousand lire would have scarcely sufficed for the keep of the horses. As for what particularly is known to me — and about which I am ready to testify under oath — I can assert — from confidences received from Mother Gattorno and because the matter was confirmed to me several times by the Count — that, for the running of his house, in the ordinary way, the Mother always paid him L. 1000 monthly. And he himself in 1895 had to tell me that he would more readily have agreed to settle the known disputes if the Mother, in place of the 1000 lire monthly, had agreed to pay him the corresponding capital. Indeed it was after I reported the matter to the Mother that she, however reluctant, confirmed the fact to me.

A similar proposal was also made directly to the Mother by her son-in-law, in the presence of one of her present secretaries — Sister Anna Camilla.

Therefore either the Count invokes legality, and then the law answers him, which proclaims the mandate gratuitous; or he invokes equity — and then the question will consist in seeing whether he can fairly ask 3000 lire a year, even if they were promised him — when, by pure liberality, at least 20,000 were given him!

II

The 13,000 lire for outlays made in the building of the novitiate were not and are not due — and consequently neither the 9,100 lire of interest.

The improbability of the fact demonstrates it first of all.

How can it be admitted that Mother Gattorno, who married her own daughter to Barbiellini, devoid of any and every means of fortune (let him prove the contrary if he can) and who therefore always had to maintain and assist him, could have conceived the idea of having him pay her debts? How can it be believed that she, who from all parts of the world always received huge aid in carrying out her wonderful work — and who sold to the Marchioness Carrega the palace of Stradone Farnese — precisely to have the means to complete the house at Piacenza — found herself in such embarrassment as to force the poor Count to sacrifice himself so much for her? And how to explain her conduct, evidently unjust and worse, consisting in never having wished to reimburse the sacrificed relative, to whom would have happened the strangest and most improbable case in the world, that of the administrator who, instead of enriching himself, becomes poorer?!

Except that the blame upon poor Mother Gattorno could not even stop here. For besides having abused his goodness of heart and generosity, she would have done worse — she would have slandered him! And indeed — speaking with me — she always maintained that she had in every case furnished Barbiellini the necessary funds, he not always remembering to use them for the stated purpose, and that she had, unfortunately, noticed that he had the receipts issued in his own name when he should have had them made out in hers.

The good lawyer Galli — a man of complete integrity — whose delicacy and honesty You, Mother, know, sends me a declaration of his from which (Annex A) it results that Mother Gattorno told him the same things, and not only — but she said them, on a certain occasion, quite clearly also to the Count's face, who did not dare to insist on his bold claim — but prudently pocketed his documents again, certain and sure that with the good nuns they would not fail to serve him another time, and especially when the Mother should come to die.

And note this strange height of impudence. In the scene narrated by Lawyer Galli, Barbiellini invoked his credits as procurator and as benefactor of the nuns, so that they would pay him a debt of his own of L. 20,000 which he had contracted with a certain Bertola — and for which he was threatened with acts of forced execution.

Well then, Mother Gattorno being dead, he writes to Galli to induce him to attest falsely that the 20,000 lire were owed by the nuns and not by him and, not content with that, denounces the Superior of the House of Piacenza as a thief of the document from which this latter state of things should have resulted!!! It is true that such a document never existed — and that the judicial authority declared the Count unworthy of belief and an exploiter of the Institute and of his mother-in-law — it is true that if the Superior herself wished it, a prosecution for slander of undoubted outcome could be instituted.

All this is true, but if one thinks that he continues undaunted in his alleged claims, one comes to wonder to what the daughters of St. Anne must find themselves exposed, if nothing on earth avails to stop his work, and if what would suffice to ruin completely any other person does not prevent him from still finding someone to listen to him!

I believe, Most Reverend Mother, that further tolerance and further pardon begin to constitute a ruinous weakness to the harm of the Institute — and that, if a luminous concurrence of proofs spared the Superior of Piacenza the pillory of public trial, it is not the case, however, to justify with this an inertia that trusts solely in the purity of conscience — while, unfortunately, human justice is not infallible like the divine.

She may meanwhile note, from the letter written by the Count to lawyer Galli, how he calls the death of Mother Gattorno enigmatic —— although no one better than he can know that she was killed by physical sufferings and by those moral tortures which he was lavishing on her with a generous and skilled hand.

And from this she may note how much there is to gain in using mercy toward him.

But, returning to the subject, it is hardly the case to observe that Barbiellini's claim is laughable — since the fact of having obtained the receipts in his own name, in the period in which he was charged with looking after the building of the Novitiate and was procurator of the nuns, has no importance, because it is a fact that depended solely on his will — and could have none — unless he demonstrated two things: 1st. That he was in a position to bear such expenses with his own money; 2nd. That of the other sums paid for the same purpose, with money received from the Mother, he was accustomed to make and did make a receipt to her.

This as to legality, for — as to the persuasion to which the Supreme Ecclesiastical Authority should come — namely, that the Count did nothing but take money with one hand and pay it with the other — and that he is creditor of nothing for the item that now occupies us — the declaration made by Lawyer Galli and what, as a matter of fact, I myself was able to declare above seem to me far and beyond sufficient, all the more in the face of the strident improbability of Barbiellini's fibs.

II.

Nothing was and nothing is owed to him for having, as he said in 1895, served the cases of Mother Gattorno and procured documents.

The cases on which he perhaps conferred with Lawyer Bignone, with lawyers Braghieri and Galli and sometimes with me, were those pending with Mrs. Tellini, daughter-in-law of Mother Gattorno, and aimed at excluding from the succession and from the family a son of hers — fraudulently made to be recognized by the wife to the husband.

The document procured by the Count was nothing other than a letter of Tellini to her husband, in which she confessed the deception made — a letter found by the Count among the papers of his brother-in-law Custo, who died during the lawsuit.

Now, Barbiellini, looking after the cases and furnishing his mother-in-law the document found, evidently did nothing but look after his own interests, working to exclude others from the Mother's succession, and to prevent a legitimate descendant of the dead brother-in-law from being able now to speak out on the position made by the Mother for her daughter Carlotta Barbiellini.

Secondly, he ought to be ashamed to ask payment for personal services rendered in favor of one who, out of pure liberality, was giving him then and after then, as an absolute minimum, a full 1000 lire monthly.

In the third place it is certain, because Mother Gattorno always said so to me, and because he himself admitted it in the talks we had, that travel expenses and other things were always advanced to the Count in large measure.

And the very size of the sum asked (10,000 lire) for some conference held and a document found would suffice to put that gentleman in his true light.

IV.

Nothing was and nothing is owed for the occupation that the nuns of Sampierdarena are said to have made of the palace situated there.

I already observed, in the Memorial of 1895, that Mother Gattorno constituted as dowry for her own daughter 80,000 lire, NOT BEARING INTEREST — guaranteed its payment with a mortgage registration on her palace of Sampierdarena, and afterward, acceding to the requests of her daughter and son-in-law, bought for 80,000 lire the property of Podenzano, which is at present in the name of Countess Barbiellini, as dotal estate. With this she obtained a discharge for the debt contracted with the dowry act — all this results from the documents that are in Your hands, Most Reverend Mother, and can easily be proved.

Barbiellini would like the nuns to have to pay him rent for having occupied for 4 years the Mother's palace in Sampierdarena, on which the mortgage was registered as guarantee of the dowry.

These are things from another world!

A mortgage is a real right constituted over the goods of the debtor to the advantage of the creditor to secure over them the satisfaction of an obligation.

The real right constituted by Mother Gattorno, with the act of 20 April 1876, drawn up by Balbi, over her property of Sampierdarena to the advantage of her son-in-law and daughter, could have no other effect than that of giving the Count and Countess the means to pay themselves, by selling the mortgaged property, when the debtor should fail in her obligation. But until this case occurred and the mortgage action was brought, Mother Gattorno had full and entire enjoyment of her own property, could dispose of it as she thought best and could even sell it and use that part of the price which might exceed the amount of the mortgage registration.

And therefore, if she thought it fitting to use it as residence for the Nuns, no one has the right to ask of these a cent of rent, much less Count Barbiellini, who ought to pay rents and not receive them, seeing and considering that his 80,000 lire were punctually paid to him and that by express agreement no interest of any kind was owed to him on that sum.

I have said that of rents he ought and ought instead to pay, and I thereby answer the last of his demands — that concerning the house in Via Merulana which he said had been occupied by the nuns.

In 1895 he admitted to me that the funds for the purchase and construction of that house had been furnished by Mother Gattorno to her daughter, and that he had had to abandon it for some time — because of disagreements arisen between him and Mr. Federico Gattorno, owner of one of the floors of the house — without, however, ceasing to occupy it with his own furniture.

And I must evidently have answered in this sense, in the memorial of 1895, his unjust claim.

And it seems obvious to me that, in the absence of a deed of gift, it would be the Count who should pay rent to the nuns.

But it is worth the trouble to mention another among the many oddities of Barbiellini's reasoning.

He asked for the rent of the house in Sampierdarena because he had a mortgage on it. But the Balbi act granted, as guarantee of the dowry, also a mortgage on the palace of Stradone Farnese in Piacenza.

And why did Barbiellini not ask also for the rent of this one? Perhaps because it was easier to deceive me by speaking of a thing almost unknown to me, while I knew very well the history and the documents of the palace of Stradone Farnese?

X

I could not, Most Reverend Mother, imagine what other claims Barbiellini may now have put forward. I know the story of the jewels, over which a suit is pending at the Tribunal of Rome, an edifying and hilarious story, in which one sees that man claim even judicially gifts. But it does not seem possible to me that he can present it also to the Sacred Council, which could not, let alone have them carried out, even approve them.

I know that he, by means of his daughter, obtained from the Mother a blank signature, alleging the need to issue a receipt in her name. I know that he then refused to return it, having his daughter say that it had been burned. I know that the Mother, before dying, fearing the abuse that could be made of her signature, thought it well to make a declaration received by the Notary Monti of Rome. I also know that the abuse took place. But I do not fear its consequences, because, by law, an obligation not written in the hand of the one who binds himself is valid only when the signature is preceded by the — Good and approved for lire etc. — in the hand of the signer. And because, besides, there would be in the fact enough to deliver the author into the hands of the King's Prosecutor.

|

I know, down to the last detail, the story of the bills of exchange signed by Barbiellini as procurator of Mother Gattorno, bills which he, she being dead, had protested against the Nuns by a so-called assignee whom he tried to deceive (See annex C) — then desisting from every act, seeing himself discovered by the one he hoped would be an accomplice.

But of this too I am not concerned, because on this fact he can only hope for silence, seeing that it already served the Investigating Judge of Piacenza to define it in a mild but effective way.

In the trial against Sister A. Giuseppa Troni it seems that it also emerged that he tried to have one of his employees say falsely that he had seen the Superior herself leave the House of the Co-witness with papers in her hand, thus establishing an iniquitous proof against an innocent woman — against whom he had already stirred up the fury of the Public Security officer, to whom he had painted the convent as a den of evildoers, while then he candidly maintains there that he never denounced the Superior, but only the fact harmful to him, which would have been attributed to her not by him, but by the Authority itself, which knew his perverse habits.

I know all this and still more, and I am therefore calm that full justice will be done to them. And a simple but perfectly logical reasoning assures me of it.

I consider that if the Count should at last wish to have recourse to the civil Authority (because the case of the jewels he cunningly had made by others), not only would he see all his demands rejected, but he would very probably set out on the broad road to Regina Coeli, with the aggravating circumstance of having to return what he had wrongly taken.

p. 793

And I think that You, Most Reverend Mother, can fear nothing from the judgment that the Sacred Council will have to render, since it cannot be guided by arid legality alone, but certainly judges from a nobler and higher point of view.

The whole debate is reduced to assertions of the Count — validly contested by the documents and by the statements of the Sisters.

And to be believed against all this one would have to be very, very pure.

Take heart, therefore, and command me always whenever you need.

Genoa, 1 June 1901.

G. BONFIGLIO

9. Letter of Federico Gattorno, dated 5 August 1895; AEFSA: A.4.54.

Federico informs the Servant of God, his sister, of the dishonest conduct of the Barbiellini; in particular he shows that Gaspare married Carlotta out of self-interest.

Rome, 5 August 1895

Dearest Sister

I received your dear letter yesterday, to which I did not reply at once because I was embarrassed as to what to tell you. Your offer of the 30 thousand that you make me, I would have liked to comply with, but at this moment it puts me in an awkward position.

If, withdrawing them now, you will not deduct from me the interest paid, I can do it, since I would have to deposit them from this moment in the Bank of Italy, which does not pay a penny of interest.

You will tell me, moreover, how I must do, because you know that I have always been ready to please you.

I have letters from Gaspare who speaks to me of selling the apartment in via Merulana in order to use the money to buy a piece of land bordering theirs at Podenzano.

I answered him that he should go ahead and that I will help him in his interest.

I never doubted that the P. would ever succeed in his aim and I predicted it to him. What grieves me most is the publicity of all the family affairs so badly denounced, which make one blush, but he has too much brazenness to take notice — Shame. For the rest, dear, the whole family is of the same blood and there is nothing to be astonished at. I remember that the Lady Countess Felicetta said that Gaspare had the right to do everything since he had made the sacrifice of marrying a Deaf-Mute. I shall never forget it; and who forced him?

E - DOCUMENTS RELATING

TO FR. GIOVANNI BATTISTA TORNATORE CM

From the beginnings of the foundation in Piacenza (1866), the Servant of God found valid spiritual and temporal help in Fr. Giovanni Battista Tornatore CM, a priest much esteemed in the diocese of Piacenza and beyond, both for his doctrine and for his virtues. When the Servant of God dismissed Don Luigi Cogrossi in 1867, Tornatore's collaboration with her became very close.

Tornatore influenced the change of the Institute's name from Daughters of Mary Immaculate to Daughters of St. Anne; he wrote the Rules of the Institute; he devoted himself to the formation of the novices; he worked with great zeal to maintain the religious spirit in the communities through visits, the preaching of Spiritual Exercises and letters, and this in full agreement with the Servant of God. Until 1888 the Circular Letters sent to the communities were signed by both.

In 1872, by order of the Holy Office, Fr. Tornatore was removed from the Institute as Author of the condemned Rules; the Servant of God worked by every means to have him reinstated and in 1875 he obtained permission to serve the Institute (cf. infra no. 4). In 1883 Tornatore was restored the faculty of receiving the sacramental confessions of the Daughters of St. Anne (cf. infra no. 7).

Around 1888 a climate of misunderstanding arose between Fr. Tornatore and the Servant of God: Tornatore believed he had authority over the Institute as its co-founder; the Servant of God did not have this concept as clear and saw the presence of two authorities as a real danger of division in the Institute, by then very extensive (cf. Summ., p. 14); therefore, after hearing the advice of several persons, among them the Servant of God Fr. Bernardino of Portogruaro and the Protector Card. Alimonda, she removed Fr. Tornatore from the Institute during the General Chapter of 1888, held under the presidency of Card. Alimonda.

After this event, undoubtedly painful for both, the relationship between the Servant of God and Fr. Tornatore remained cordial and constant until his death on 31 January 1895, as attested by Fr. Tornatore's letters to the Foundress and various letters of hers to Count Francesco Caracciolo (the letters of the Servant of God to Fr. Tornatore have not come down to us).

1. Letter of Fr. Tornatore, undated; AFSA: A.1.0.

Fr. Tornatore tells a Daughter of St. Anne about the foundation and the change of name of the Institute and the drawing up of the Rules.

My Daughter blessed in Jesus

I received your letter written on the 4th instant; and you tell me that you received mine. First of all I must tell you the pain I feel at learning that in the Institute of the Daughters of the Holy Mother so little prayer is made and so little love given to my angel, the venerable Father Bernardo Maria Clausi. And yet He is the one whom the Lord used to found the Institute.

You will say to me: and in what way did the Venerable Father Bernardo found the Institute? If I have not told you at other times, I tell you now. At the beginning, when the Mother came to Piacenza to found an Institute, she came with some daughters, and they were called the Daughters of Mary Immaculate and were directed by a certain Priest named Don Luigi Cogrossi.

Knowing that the Mother and these daughters of hers were poor, I brought them an alms of one hundred lire; although I remember the sum, the Mother, as soon as she saw me, became attached to me in a way that it is impossible for me to describe to you: immediately she placed herself under my direction; then I made known to her my devotion to my angel, Father Bernardo; and I made known to her that my servant of God had inspired me, for several years, to found an Institute of Daughters of St. Anne, and that therefore, if she wished to be directed by me, it was good that the Daughters, instead of being called Daughters of Mary, be called Daughters of St. Anne, Mother of Mary Immaculate. The Lord, to make known to the Mother that this was His will, caused the Holy Mother St. Anne and her faithful servant the Venerable Father Bernardo to appear to the Mother and make known to her that it was the pleasure of God that the Institute be the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne.

In this vision the venerable one held in his hand the book of the Rules and told the Mother that I had that book and that she should have it given to her by me. Behold, daughter, how the Institute was founded; and behold how the venerable Father Bernardo was as the minister whom the Lord and the holy Mother used to found the Institute. I then made the Rules; these Rules, because of the calumnies of my enemies, were burned by order of the holy office. The Mother said: the burned Rules, made by the Father, will come out of the fire; and this was a prophecy; because although many set their hand to making new Rules, they never succeeded; so that again, by the will of our Cardinal Protector, Cardinal Berardi, I had to make them; and they are the common rules which they have now. You see, then, daughter, how true it is that the Daughters of St. Anne should be very devoted to the Venerable Father Bernardo, my angel? oh how many graces they would receive if they prayed to him! Pray to him yourself and say to him every day some Our Father and insinuate this devotion to your sisters. Keep this letter very reserved; and so, speaking with prudent Sisters, you will be able to make known to them the origin of the Institute [...].

Jesus, your heart, I am your Father

Gio. BATTA T., missionary 2. Letter of the Servant of God, dated 8 January 1871; AFSA: A.2.19.

The Servant of God writes to the Superior General of the Priests of the Mission and sets out the situation of the Institute; the principal artisan of this work is Fr. Tornatore of the Alberoni College of Piacenza: she therefore asks that he release him from obedience to his local superior so that he may devote himself entirely to the Institute.

To the Rev. Superior General of the Missionaries

Rev. Superior General,

Since the surest way is to turn to the source, from which grace must spring, this unworthy servant of the Lord, forgetting her nothingness, sends to Your Reverence this supplication, in order to obtain what she here sets before You. God caused to be born in the Church a new Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, Mother of the Immaculate, four years ago, and with the blessing of the Most High it prospers, counting a large number of Religious. The Houses are three, the fourth is about to open. The functions are: the assistance of the sick at home, in the Hospitals, of both sexes; taking in poor girls in danger, who run the risk of losing their honor, and giving them that Christian and moral education which suits them. A boys' school for children of low condition free of charge and, indeed, when possible, they are given that little bit of food, as a second asylum; the perpetual Adoration of Jesus in the Sacrament day and night. It was blessed by the Church, granting to our Oratories rather extensive faculties. The Holy Pope Pius IX has our Rules, as also the Holy Congregation, from which, in better time, the approval will come. The Common ones have long been printed with the approval of the Diocesan, Monsignor Bishop Count Ranza, from whom Your Reverend Lordship to condescend to what, humbled at your feet, I ask You, being unable to go there in person because of my frail health; and it is this that, with such anxiety, urges me to order everything with the help of God. All this was done by a Son of Yours, by the Rev. Mr. Tornatore; I serve him only as Your miserable instrument. He now holds the post of professor in the Alberoni College; this year the Classes end, and now nothing else is needed except that Your Reverend Lordship deign to send two lines containing Your Obedience, dedicating him to the care of this Institute, removing him from the Obedience of Your local Superior and remaining subject only to Your Reverend Lordship.

p. 805

He is too necessary to this Community. Know that we are directed by his sons, who received the command from the Diocesans. Grant, for charity's sake, the prayer of this poor creature, who in the name of the whole Community earnestly begs Your Reverend Lordship to deign to grant me in this my request.

May Your Reverend Lordship send Your paternal blessing to one who humbly awaits it and respectfully awaits it, while she declares herself of Your Reverend Lordship

Most humble Sister ANNA MARIA

Piacenza, 8 January 1871 Rosa GATTORNO

Most Rev. Excellency

It would have been my duty to come before now to inform you of all that I did, about the matter known to Your Most Rev. Excellency, who with such charity deigned to send me the letter of recommendation. I would have wished keenly to come to Your Most Rev. 5. Testimonial letter of the ven. Giovanni Battista Scalabrini, bishop of Piacenza, dated 4 March 1876; AFSA: A.1.0.

The ven. G.B. Scalabrini, as soon as he assumed the exercise of pastor of the Church of Piacenza, was able to enjoy the association of the Daughters of St. Anne, which flourishes through the zeal and industry of the Foundress Rosa Gattorno; he also gathered information on the priest Giovanni Battista Tornatore CM, member of the Academy of St. Thomas Aquinas, rector in temporalibus of the Daughters of St. Anne; he rejects the accusations made against him and praises his doctrine and zeal.

Mons. Gio. Batta Scalabrini, Prelate of His Holiness Our Lord,

Domestic and Assistant at the Pontifical Throne, by the grace of

God and of the Apostolic See Bishop and Count of Piacenza and

immediately subject to the same Holy See.

Having been recently, though unworthy, raised to the See of Piacenza and having soon assumed the exercise of Pastor and of paternal solicitude toward this same most beloved Spouse, which the Supreme Pastor J.C. Our Lord, with his most precious Blood perpetually united to himself, entrusted to us to cultivate, turning our thought to those chosen ones, of whom the more exalted the glory, the greater must be the care of the Pastor, it was given us to enjoy in Christ that most pious Association called of the Daughters of St. Anne, and which, through the zeal and industry of the beloved sister in J. Christ Rosa Gattorno, author of the same Association, so abundantly flourishes in this City and Diocese, and with how much fruit of souls and progress of girls of the weaker sex in true faith, piety and religion, God knows, and we saw with our own eyes.

Since then we recognized that a greater fruit was to be hoped for in the future from the aforesaid Association if to its spiritual government there were appointed an Ecclesiastic well informed of the spirit with which it was born and grew.

And since from opportune information we are certain that the M.R.D. Giovanni Batta Tornatore, Priest of the Mission of St. Vincent de Paul, Lecturer in Sacred Theology in this V. Alberoni College and for many years Rector in temporalibus of the aforesaid Association, is endowed, and that, having had him come before us and examined by ourselves with the usual formalities, diligently and with severity in the Lord, we found him wise in the philosophical, theological, moral and ascetical sciences, so that we rightly had to hold erroneous and as such reject the judgment of some who, moved indeed by zeal but not by science, defamed him as fallen into errors.

Therefore we, of certain knowledge, to all those whom the present fact may concern, in whatever way bear witness and attest that the aforesaid Rev. Gio. Battista Tornatore, Priest of the Mission of St. Vincent de Paul, Lecturer in Sacred Theology at the V. Alberoni College, and Director in temporalibus of the Daughters of St. Anne as above, is so distinguished by integrity of life and morals that he is commonly known by the term Saint, for piety, religious zeal, for very great devotion toward the Holy See and the Vicar of O.L.J.C., commendable as for all the other virtues that befit an Ecclesiastic, gifted in talent and doctrine, a follower of right principles in the philosophical disciplines, a Thomist in Dogmatics, a Liguorian in Moral Theology, in Ascetics, in turn, averse to reprobated mysticism, so that he deserved to be counted among the Members of the Academy of St. Thomas Aquinas instituted in Rome and approved by the authority of the reigning Supreme Pontiff Pius IX, as we can attest from the diploma of his admission delivered to us.

Therefore we gladly accompany in the Lord with these our Letters the same Priest Tornatore, for every effect of reason and of favor. In witness whereof

Given in Piacenza from the Palace of our residence

On 4 March 1876

signed Gio. BATTISTA Bishop

6. Letter of the ven. G.B. Scalabrini, dated 11 April 1877; ACVP:

Daughters of St. Anne.

The ven. Scalabrini thanks Card. Giuseppe Berardi because he is working to reinstate Fr. Tornatore in the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne; he examined Fr. Tornatore carefully and ascertained the falsity of the accusations brought against him; the condemned Rules had been examined by a commission of theologians appointed by his predecessor.

Most Eminent Most Reverend

I can only applaud Your Eminence's thought for the reinstatement of Fr. Tornatore as spiritual Director of the Daughters of St. Anne, not only in the interest of the pious Institute, of which he is Co-founder, but also for my comfort, for not without pain can I see humiliated with the note of suspect doctrines this man, Professor of Moral Theology, respected, esteemed and well-liked not only by his Superiors and Confreres, but also by this Clergy, while the greater and more respectable part of it vies to have him as counselor and spiritual Director.

Therefore, as soon as I entered upon the governing of this Church, prejudiced against him by what had been reported to me about him, to resolve my wavering spirit I called Tornatore to me, in Rome depressed, in Piacenza esteemed and revered, and nicknamed the Saint, and subjected him to a diligent examination to ascertain his principles in the philosophical, theological, moral and ascetical sciences, and I was able to console myself on finding Tornatore's doctrine in everything conformable to that of the Catholic Church, and thus to convince myself of the falsity of the accusations brought against him, and to touch with my hand that the esteem which the Piacentines had of Tornatore was well founded; wherefore I promptly transmitted to the Holy See testimonial letters in his favor, which, however, had no effect whatever.

That if the Holy Congregation charged with the examination of the Rules of that pious Institute found something to say on various points of them, in my view not to Tornatore but rather to the Commission, to which by my Predecessor those were submitted for examination and approval, should be attributed whatever in them was found less suited to the governance of the Daughters of St. Anne; and I would say almost to my Predecessor himself, who thought fit to affix his signature to them.

Your Eminence will do a very meritorious work both for the Daughters of St. Anne in general, of whom you are Protector, and in a special way for this Mother House, which, being for a great part of the year abandoned by the Superior General, needs a man of God who knows its spirit and forms the postulants and novices.

I trust that my wishes, thanks to the concern of Your Eminence, will be granted, doing justice to Father Tornatore, who should no longer remain under the weight of false accusations while he exercises on a large scale the holy ministry in this my Diocese, a ministry which I should prevent if they were well founded.

Your Eminence will not lack means of drawing the attention of the Holy Father to this matter and of finding a way to bring it happily to its conclusion. Kissing your hand, I profess myself with the deepest veneration

Gio. BATTISTA Bishop

F - DOCUMENTS RELATING TO THE APOSTOLIC VISIT

The Institute had only one Apostolic Visit, carried out by Abbot Domenico Serafini, later cardinal, from 1898 to 1903.

Some years earlier there had been another intervention of the ecclesiastical Authority to which Pope Leo XIII did not wish to give an official character. In 1889, in fact, an anonymous letter had reached the Holy Father denouncing disorders among the Daughters of St. Anne, especially in the general house in Rome (cf. infra no. 1); the Pope directed that the Cardinal Protector appoint Mons. Beniamino Cavicchioni as Delegate to the Institute, thus avoiding the appointment of an Apostolic Visitor (cf. infra nos. 2 and 3). Mons. Cavicchioni visited only the houses of Rome (cf. Summ., p. 81) and dealt with some affairs of the Institute, but no traces are found of measures taken by him, either in the Archive of the Institute or in the Archive of the Congregation for Religious. In May 1891 Cardinal Alimonda died and Card. Isidoro Verga, Prefect of the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars, was appointed Protector of the Institute, so that Mons. Cavicchioni's commission lapsed.

In 1898 Abbot Domenico Serafini OSB was appointed Apostolic Visitor of the Institute (cf. infra no. 4). The letter of appointment indicates as the reason for the measure «various inconveniences» occurring in the Institute; among these only the printing of a book for the use of the Sisters is specified: it is the volume Travagli e conforti dell'anima nel cammino della perfezione [Labors and Comforts of the Soul on the Path of Perfection], written by the Foundress and printed at the instance of Princess Emilia di Fitalia (cf. Summ. pp. 6, 445, depositions of Card. Gennaro Granito di Belmonte and of Princess di Fitalia; Votum of Fr. Paolino Zavarella).

The tension in relations between Card. Isidoro Verga and the Servant of God may have influenced the causes of the measure, because of the inconveniences that arose since the cardinal showed an excessive fondness for a young sister assigned to the general secretariat (cf. Summ., pp. 33-34, deposition of Card. Granito di Belmonte).

In 1899 Card. Verga died. The Apostolic Visitor, in his deposition at the Roman Process, states that on this occasion the Servant of God «tried to shake off» the Apostolic Visit. No document has been found proving this assertion. On the contrary, it is established that it was the Visitor himself who feared that the Apostolic Visit would be suspended: in this sense he wrote, on 12 August 1899, to Don Felice Cavagnis, secretary of the Congregation for Extraordinary Ecclesiastical Affairs, asking him to take an interest and to intervene «for fear of a coup de main». Following this letter, the Holy Father, in the audience of 22 August 1899, suspended the appointment of the Protector and ordered the continuation of the Apostolic Visit (cf. infra no. 7).

p. 815

The Visit continued even after the death of the Servant of God, which occurred on 6 May 1900, and concluded in 1903.

The main observation the Visitor made to the Servant of God concerned the administration of the Institute. In his concluding report he notes the soundness of the Institute from the economic point of view and acknowledges, praising it, the great rectitude of the Servant of God in administration (cf. infra no. 8).

This assessment removes all foundation from the accusations made against the Servant of God.
