8. Report of the Apostolic Visitor, dated 1 March 1903; ACRIS: P.31.

In this concluding report the Apostolic Visitor's judgment on the economic state of the Institute is relevant, removing all foundation from the accusations made against the Servant of God.

Report of the sacred Apostolic Visit made to the Institute

of the Daughters of St. Anne by Mons. Domenico Serafini O.S.B.

Archbishop of Spoleto

1. By Decree of the Holy Congregation of Bishops and Regulars dated 9 July 1898 No. 10791 the undersigned, then Abbot General of the Cassinese Congregation of the primitive observance, was appointed Apostolic Visitor of the Institute Daughters of St. Anne, approved by the Holy See.

2. The Institute being very widespread not only in Europe, but also in America and in Africa, it seemed to the Visitor impossible, and perhaps even useless, to visit all and each of the houses: firstly because the greater part of the houses are composed of three or four Sisters only; secondly because the temporal Administration of them is in the hands of the lay civil authorities who called them; finally because it could easily be understood that the evils and disturbances which seemed to afflict the Institute had their origin rather in the general government and in the direction given to the Institute itself than in the running of the individual houses. Therefore the undersigned Visitor thought it well to visit first the principal houses of Italy, reserving to himself afterward to take those decisions that might subsequently seem opportune.

3. In July of the same year 1898 the Mother house of Piacenza was visited, where in the summer the Mother General and foundress Rosa Gattorno resided, and where the Novitiate for Upper Italy is located. In the following December the General house of Rome in Via Merulana was visited, where the Novitiate for central Italy is. In June of the following year 1899 the visit was made to the Novitiate house of Naples and that of Palermo, and at the same time other houses were visited which were found on the way, or which it was thought convenient to visit. In November and December of the same year the principal houses of Liguria and Piedmont were visited.

4. The undersigned would have continued in the spring the visit of other houses if his appointment as Archbishop of Spoleto and therefore the cares of the government of the Diocese, always difficult at the beginning, had not prevented him.

5. At the same time, on 6 May 1900, the Mother General and Foundress of the Institute, Sister Anna Rosa Gattorno, came to death in the house of Rome; therefore it was necessary to proceed to the appointment of the new Superior General. With the consent of the Most Eminent Card. Rampolla, Protector of the Institute, the General Chapter was held in Rome in the month of October of the same year, which was presided over, in the name of the Most Eminent Protector, by the undersigned Apostolic Visitor. In the said Chapter Sister Anna Benedetta Carrega, formerly Secretary of the deceased, was canonically elected Superior General. The Secretaries, the Assistants and the Provincials were also appointed according to the Constitutions. The whole proceeded with order and tranquility and with common satisfaction.

'

6. After this the Institute began to take a more regular course. The new M. General was of common liking to the Sisters. The relations with the relatives of the late Gattorno, which had cost so much trouble and annoyance, were, not without difficulty, smoothed over, at least for now. Finally the government of the Cong., which under the late General had been too personal, began to proceed more in conformity with the Constitutions. Hence the task of the Apostolic Visitor seems now exhausted, and should the Holy Cong. think it opportune it could cease altogether.

7. The undersigned, before laying in the hands of that Holy Cong. the charge entrusted to him of the Holy Visit, thinks it his duty to set out briefly what he has been able to gather concerning the personal, economic and moral state of the Institute and to submit subordinately what he believes most advantageous for the regular running of the Institute itself.

I

Personal state

8. The Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne is at present composed of about two hundred seventy-two houses, in which live about five thousand professed Sisters of both annual vows and perpetual vows. 9. The said houses are divided into seven Provinces: General house, which includes the Roman province. Mother house of Piacenza, which forms the province of Upper Italy.

Provincial house of Naples, to which belong the houses of the Neapolitan region, Apulia, Abruzzi and Calabria.

Provincial house of Palermo, which embraces all the houses of Sicily.

Provincial house of Pará, to which are subject all the houses of Brazil.

Provincial house of La Paz, on which depend the houses of Bolivia and Chile.

Provincial house of Sucre, on which depend other houses of Bolivia and that of Lower Peru.

10. It is to be noted that the houses of Africa, four in number (Italian Colony), two in Spain, two in France and the house in Sardinia depend directly on the general house.

11. Of all these houses, only twenty-eight are the property of the Institute; the other houses belong to Congregations of charity, to municipalities or also to private persons or to civilly unrecognized Institutes, which maintain the Sisters there.

p. 828

II

Economic state

12. In the houses that are not the property of the Institute, the Sisters support themselves with the allowances given them by the local Administrations, which are established by regular contract between the Mother General and the respective Administrators. In general these houses have enough to live comfortably and to make savings. The local Superior every half-year is required to send to the Mother General a small statement of the Community's income and expenses together with the surplus. These surpluses constitute the principal revenue of the Institute, and in 1901 they reached the sum of L. 211,499.40.

13. The twenty-eight houses owned by the Institute support themselves with some legacies assigned to particular houses, with the work and occupations of the Sisters, with subsidies and in a few places with begging: this is done in the houses of Bassano Veneto, Lodi, Florence, Prato, Pistoia, Siena and Pisa. It would be desirable that begging cease gradually as the houses can support themselves with other resources. The Mother General, moreover, in extraordinary cases gives subsidies from the common fund of the Institute.

14. The Novitiate houses of Rome and Piacenza, which do not have sufficient income to maintain a large Community, such as habitually lives in them, are assisted by the Mother General with the common funds of the Institute. 15. The general fund is formed: a) by the dowries of the postulants; b) by the surpluses of the individual houses;

c) by the warehouse and store of habits etc., which each house acquires for the Sisters;

d) by the income of the property called Gargatano near Piacenza;

e) by income in bonds left by the foundress;

f) by extraordinary subsidies.

16. In 1901 the debts were reduced to L. 200,000 with the Bank of Italy, mortgaged on the general house of Rome, and to L. 200,000 with the Savings Bank of Genoa, mortgaged on the Gargatano estate. There are other small debts of little importance. The annual interest is regularly paid, and nonetheless the 1901 budget closed with a surplus of L. 50,771.14.

17. From what has been set out so far it can be concluded that the late foundress Rosa Gattorno left Her Institute solidly established and in a flourishing state on the economic side. After this the undersigned thinks it superfluous to dwell now on some irregularities which he found in Gattorno's Administration, irregularities which with her death have ceased to exist. Moreover, if Gattorno, being foundress of the Institute and by reason of the prestige she enjoyed over the Sisters, thought it permissible to act with a certain freedom and independence in administering the goods of the Institute, goods which for the most part she had herself procured for it, the fact has shown that She had at heart the advantage of the Institute above every other thing. The very way in which she, in the last months of her life, secured the patrimony of the Institute against possible claims of those who might perhaps have dared to claim a part of it, shows the rectitude of her intentions even where the affection of a mother found itself in hard contrast with the duties of a religious Superior. At present the Administration proceeds regularly and no complaints on this subject have reached the undersigned.

III

Moral state

18. The religious development of the Institute does not seem to have been equal to its material development, and manifold complaints reached the Holy See about disorders occurring within it. The undersigned makes it his duty to set out what he has been able to ascertain, in sacred visit, concerning the religious and moral state of the Institute.

I. - The little religious spirit of the Daughters of St. Anne has been lamented: nor is it a matter for wonder. Since the principal income of the Institute comes from the surplus of the houses, in which the Sisters are maintained by public administrations (this surplus was in 1901 L. 211,499.40), which is regularly sent to the general house, it happened that from the beginning an effort was made to multiply such houses, increasing the number of sisters as much as possible. All this was done to the detriment of the religious education of the sisters, who sometimes, after three or four months of any Novitiate whatever, were assigned to be part of these small Communities, where it is not easy even for well-grounded Religious to maintain the first fervor. At present things have improved, His Eminence Card. Verga, of blessed memory, Protector of the Institute, having imposed that the Novitiate of the Sisters be a whole year. If the Superiors are more cautious in future in accepting postulants and in admitting to profession it is to be hoped that the improvement will continue.

II. - Moreover the Novitiate itself did not always correspond to the spiritual needs of the postulants. In the Novitiate of Rome some years ago the study of vocal and instrumental music had been introduced, and entertainments and academies were sometimes given, with real dissipation of the religious: now this has been given up. In the Novitiate of Naples the Novices are compelled to go often to accompany the dead, with much bodily toil and little spiritual gain. The Novitiate of Palermo is established in the house in via d'Ossuna, where a College for young girls of the Aristocracy is open, from contact with which the postulants, for the most part of humble condition and destined for humble offices, will not draw much advantage. It would rather be desirable that the Novitiate houses be separate from Colleges, public schools, hospitals etc., so that the Novices might occupy themselves with greater recollection in their own exercises.

III. - When the time of the Novitiate is over, the Novices are admitted to annual vows which are renewed for about nine years until perpetual vows are made. In the past the renewal of vows depended on the Mother General, who could suspend it for one or more years in punishment of faults; indeed sometimes she even deprived the guilty Sister of the religious habit. These provisions often increased the complaints and did not contribute to the amendment of undisciplined Sisters; so it seemed fitting to the undersigned to forbid the Superior General to use such means of correction; but rather, when sisters were known to be insubordinate and incorrigible, according to the Constitutions they should be dismissed.

IV. - The longing to increase the number of small houses has meant that foundations disadvantageous to the Sisters and to the Institute were sometimes accepted. The undersigned thought it opportune from the beginning of the Holy Visit to forbid the M. General to establish new Communities without his particular permission, and he judges that in future too it will be useful to restrain somewhat the desire to open new houses before the number of suitable sisters is proportionally increased. It was also expedient to order the closing of some already opened house, for example the Syphilis hospital of Trapani, because, also on the Bishop's advice, it was of grave moral danger to the Sisters.

V. - The greater part of the houses, as was said, are composed of few religious (three or four approximately), under the dependence of Congregations of charity or other lay institutes, which, all intent on the economic good of the works administered by them, care little or nothing for the spiritual and material good of the sisters, whom they strive to exploit for the profit of the works themselves. Sometimes these houses are situated in places where, because of the deficiency of the clergy, it is not possible to find a spiritual director suited to maintain the religious spirit in the Sisters. What wonder if in such conditions of things some sister loses her first fervor? It belongs to the prudence of the M. General to choose more solid Sisters for the more difficult houses, changing them from time to time. In general care should be taken that at least every two years all the Sisters without exception make a course of spiritual exercises of ten or fifteen days, in a central house of the province, as prescribed in the Constitutions.

VI. - The choice of Superiors of the Communities has often given rise to disturbances and discontent — both with regard to the persons and with regard to the length of the Superiorship. The large number of Communities established in so short a time produced the need to find many Superiors; and the choice was not always happy. As the number of experienced Sisters grows, the difficulties are diminishing. It would be desirable that from now on only Sisters professed of perpetual vows be chosen as Superiors, and that ordinarily the Superiors remain in office for a triennium, with faculty for the Superior General to confirm them for further trienniums, if the advantage of the community required it and the spiritual good of the superior did not require otherwise.

VII. - An occasion of grave complaints has been the treatment of the sick Sisters, especially the chronic ones, who are not lacking in an Institute where material labors are heavy and sometimes excessive. Since they cannot be placed in the houses dependent on Administrations external to the Institute, because the Administrators would hardly grant it, two houses were established in Italy to which to send them: one in Naples, the other at Gargatano near Piacenza. The house in Naples, situated in one of the filthiest quarters of the city, in a poorly aired place amid vulgar people, was ordered closed by the undersigned. The house at Gargatano, although in better condition than that of Naples, does not seem suited to the purpose of a house of health, being situated in the midst of the countryside, with a very harsh climate in winter, and without many spiritual comforts, a good Parish Priest from the neighborhood acting as Chaplain and Director, who goes there from time to time. In this house, when the undersigned made the sacred visit, there were about twenty Sisters, the greater part sick, the others sent there in penance. Such a mixture did not seem fitting for maintaining in the community that spirit of peace and charity which would be so necessary for the poor sick. It would therefore be desirable that in each province a central house be established for the chronic sick in a healthy place, near a city, where spiritual and bodily aids can easily be procured, and that the sick there be assisted with all charity by Sisters of good spirit.

VII. - In the economic administration of the houses it has sometimes been complained that the Superiors treated their subjects badly, saving more than they ought in order to send more abundant surpluses to the central fund of the Institute. At times these surpluses were in part sent to the M. General as a particular gift, thinking to do something pleasing to her. The undersigned disapproved this practice, and has reason to believe that after Gattorno's death it has ceased. Yet it would not be useless to remind the Superiors that in the half-yearly accounts the surpluses they send to the central fund must be recorded in full, nor is it lawful for Superiors to make gifts in money or otherwise to persons belonging to the Institute or outside it, outside the cases foreseen by the Constitutions and permitted by the Apostolic Decrees.

IX. - Finally the undersigned declares that he has carried out the orders of the Holy Cong. by withdrawing all copies of the book entitled: «Labors and Consolations of the soul on the Way of Perfection described by a Servant of God», as far as it was possible for him. He can moreover assure that the said book has left no bad effects in the Sisters, its reading not having been widely spread nor easy of understanding to the greater part of the Sisters.

In concluding the present report the undersigned thinks it his duty to declare that, notwithstanding the defects noted above and those others which are inseparable from every human society, however perfect, he has found in the Daughters of St. Anne in general a spirit of abnegation and humility, submission to Superiors and will to do good; so that there is hope that, with the Constitutions approved by the Holy See ever better observed and the abuses mentioned removed, as has already been done in great part, the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne will continue to bear fruits of salvation and edification ever more abundant in the Church of God.

Spoleto, 1 March 1903.

Apostolic Visitor of the Daughters of St. Anne
